reply:
As Minister of State at the Department of Transport with special responsibility for Rural Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to rural public transport service provision; however, I am not involved in the day-to-day operations.
The National Transport Authority (NTA) has statutory responsibility for securing and monitoring the provision of public passenger transport services nationally, including the Connecting Ireland Rural Mobility Plan and TFI Local Link services. In light of the NTA responsibilities I have referred your question to the NTA for direct reply to you. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within ten working days.

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on Ireland's operation and implementation of the EU Migration and Asylum Pact.
reply:
The International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.
The Department undertook significant preparation prior to commencement, developing and resourcing new processes and procedures to ensure readiness for the new timelines required under the Pact. The new system has been in place for almost four months and is operating as intended.
At the front end of the process, screening, registration and pathway allocation are functioning effectively, with statutory timelines being met and cases successfully channelled into the appropriate procedural pathways. Early data also suggests that screening under the new framework is being successfully operationalised at scale, with 2,427 applicants for international protection commencing screening and 2,113 completing screening between 12 June and 23 September 2026.
The Pact has strengthened our ability to establish identity and assess vulnerabilities at an early stage. Enhanced screening measures, improved document verification capabilities, and more effective use of electronic evidence are supporting more robust and informed decision-maki

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will consider options (details supplied) regarding SMEs with under 100 employees, and the crime they face.
reply:
I take any risk to retailers, retail staff and communities very seriously. That is why the Government is taking a range of strategic, operational and legislative measures to address retail crime.
The Programme for Government contains a number of commitments in this area and a range of further measures are under consideration. They include an expansion of the use of community sanctions for retail crime and updating public order legislation to enable courts to exclude prolific offenders from retail premises for a specified period.
My Department is currently finalising a Retail Crime Strategy, which is at an advanced stage of development. I expect to receive a draft shortly and intend to publish the Strategy in the coming months.
Broader Government initiatives relating to community safety, youth justice, probation supervision, antisocial behaviour, increased Garda recruitment and enhanced high-visibility policing will also contribute to reducing retail crime and supporting retailers, staff and customers. In addition, An Garda Síochána is developing a new Crime Prevention and Reduction Strategy for 2026-2029.
Regarding the Adult Cautioning Scheme, this is a non-statutory scheme agreed between, and administered by, An Garda Síochána and the Director of Public Prosecutions. Both bodies are independent in the exercise of their functions and I have no role in determining the criteria governing the operation of the Scheme.
Supports for retailers falls under the Department for Enterpri

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when there will be a roll out of a new youth justice strategy; and the priorities his Department will focus on.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 44 and 75 together.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. The core exchequer and dormant account funding allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled since 2020, standing at a record €43 million.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. It follow operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of YDPs throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
An evaluation of the YDPs was commissioned in 2022 and published in June 2023 concluding that YDPs are performing well in many areas that are known to impact positively on reducing crime and reoffending.
There has been an estimated 20% reduction in youth offences referred to An Garda Síochána between 2020 and 2025; with this decrease taking place during a period of population growth in the 12-17 cohort. Youth Diversion Projects work with more than 4,500 young people each year, resulting in thousands of young people diverted from criminal pathways, which then leads to fewer victims and

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when he expects to publish the draft National Migration and Integration Strategy; and if it will include consideration of an all-island approach to the management of migration.
reply:
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to publish a National Migration and Integration Strategy setting out how the Government intends to respond to the demands and opportunities facing Ireland's society and economy over the next decade.
My Department is currently working collaboratively with a wide range of Government Departments to develop this Strategy, with the aim of publishing Ireland's first overarching, whole-of-government National Migration and Integration Strategy in the coming months.
The scope of the Strategy will include issues such as social impacts, labour market needs, legal pathways, international education and planning for public service provision, including housing, among other migration-related issues. While the Strategy cannot extend beyond matters within the State's control, it will recognise the importance of Irish migration policy accounting for developments elsewhere, including in Northern Ireland and the Common Travel Area generally, as well as migration policy development within the European Union. This is particularly important in protecting the Common Travel Area and ensuring the free movement of citizens between Ireland and the United Kingdom.
To support this work, a Strategic Migration Policy Group (SMPG) was established in December 2024. The Group now comprises ten Government Departments meeting at senior official level.
Each Department is in a position to convey the perspectives of the agencies under its remit, which have also prov

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the categories of harmful and violent material that will be covered by the forthcoming legislation criminalising the possession, production, and distribution of extreme pornography; and to provide an update on the proposed scope of the legislation.
reply:
In July, I secured Government approval to draft legislation to criminalise the possession, production and distribution of extreme or violent pornography, addressing a significant gap in Irish law. Such material is having a harmful impact, particularly on young people, and is distorting healthy sexual development and contributing to misogynistic attitudes.
The proposed offences will criminalise extreme or violent pornographic material, including depictions of rape or violence causing serious harm to a person and depictions of bestiality or necrophilia. It is intended to set out specific categories of such extreme or violent content, which will be defined during the drafting process.
In developing this proposal, my Department has considered a range of sources, including the Resolution 1835 (2011) of the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly on violent and extreme pornography and a review of approaches in other jurisdictions. All of these sources have informed development of the proposal to date. The specifics of the approach will be further examined, with the benefit of advice from the Office of the Attorney General. The timeline will depend on completion of drafting, the publication of the Bill and its subsequent passage through the Oireachtas.
My aim is to craft offences that are clear and specific in meeting the policy goal of combatting the most extreme and violent forms of pornography, which will allow such material to readily be identified and acted upon, while also en

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he is aware of work ongoing in the Cork Detention Barracks; the nature of the work; and the amount that has been spent in the past 12-months in the building.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 49 and 72 together.

Since 2024, 292 spaces have been constructed across the prison estate, with 126 delivered in 2024, 106 in 2025 and a further 60 so far in 2026. question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the funding allocated to An Garda Síochána in Budget 2027; and the priorities for the use of the same.
reply:
Under Budget 2027, I have secured record funding of €5.9 billion for the Justice Sector.
The Garda Vote will receive the funding required to provide for the equipment, technology, facilities, fleet and personnel needed to support An Garda Síochána's vital policing efforts.
Under Section 33 of the Policing, Security and Community Safety Act 2025, the Garda Commissioner is responsible for the operation and management of the Garda organisation. Furthermore, under Section 72 of the 2025 Act, the Garda Commissioner is the accounting officer for the organisation and is responsible for the allocation and management of the Garda Vote.
Further details regarding the breakdown of funding allocated across the Justice Sector, including to An Garda Síochána, will be released later this week as part of the Budget 2027 announcement.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to provide an update on the progress being made to resolve the solicitors' dispute over the introduction of the new criminal legal aid scheme.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 70 together.
The reform of the criminal legal aid fee structure in the District Court is designed to improve efficiencies, reduce unnecessary adjournments, simplify the administration of criminal legal aid, speed up case resolution and enable faster payments to practitioners through the repeal of previous regulations and the provision of new regulatory arrangements.
Since the commencement of the new system, and as of 2 October, almost 2,400 new certificates (invoices for payment) for legal aid have issued with an approximate total value of €1.25 million in the District Court alone.
It should be noted that, under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. My Department has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Under the Courts Service Act 1998, the management and administration of the courts is a matter for the Courts Service, while the allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and the management of court lists are matters for the Judiciary, in particular the Presidents of the Courts.
Of the cases concluded under the new system, since 1st July 2026, 75% concluded with one appearance only in court and 99% of concluded cases were finalised within five appearances. Previously, where a case concluded in one appearance, the solicitor was paid appr

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason he overturned in excess of 500 deportation orders last year.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based. The enforcement provisions of our immigration laws, including deportation orders, are an essential component of an effective system and help to ensure public confidence in the fair and consistent application of our legislation.
Deportations are often costly and complex to carry out. Where a person does not remove themselves from the State following the making of a deportation order, they may be removed. My Department has taken significant steps to strengthen immigration enforcement measures and increase the number of removals.
The number of deportation orders signed in 2024 (2,403) represented an increase of 180% compared with 2023 (857). In 2025, 4,700 deportation orders were signed, an increase of 96% compared with 2024. As of 2 October 2026, 3,538 deportation orders have been signed.
In 2024, 1,122 people departed the State through various mechanisms, including enforced deportation and voluntary return. In 2025, the departure of 2,111 people was confirmed through these pathways, an increase of 88% compared with 2024. As of 2 October 2026, 1,809 people have departed the State through these pathways.
Section 3(11) of the Immigration Act 1999, as amended, provides that a deportation order may be revoked and my Department receives submissions from people seeking that this provision be invoked.
In assessing such submissions, consideration is given to whether there is compelling new info

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Cearúil asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken by his Department and An Garda Síochána to prevent and reduce anti-social behaviour in communities; and the initiatives currently in place to address issues such as public disorder, dangerous driving, and the misuse of fireworks.
reply:

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the position regarding any allowances being considered for people legally resident in Ireland and in the process of meeting the requirements for Irish citizenship in the context of imminent changes in citizenship requirements.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities, and the economy.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable.
The proposed changes do not seek to restrict integration or exclude migrants from Irish society. Rather, they are intended to ensure that citizenship reflects a genuine and lasting connection to Ireland, an understanding of the State and its institutions, and an ongoing commitment to Irish society.
While the proposals may affect the timeframe within which some individuals become eligible to apply for citizenship, they do not affect a person's entitlement to reside, work, study, establish a business or establish a life in Ireland in accordance with the terms of their immigration permission.

question: Deputy Ruairí Ó Murchú asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current average processing times for international protection applicants; and the progress being made to reduce the processing times for international protection applicants.
reply:
It is a central priority for me that Ireland’s immigration system is robust and rules based.
There has been a significant increase in investment in the international protection system over the last number of years which, combined with digitisation and process re-engineering, has facilitated a major increase in processing capacity and demonstrates a strong commitment to reducing cases on hand.
In 2025, the International Protection Office (IPO) delivered over 20,200 first instance decisions compared to approximately 14,100 in 2024: a 44% increase. IPAT more than doubled the number of appeals closed from 3,100 in 2024 to nearly 6,300 in 2025. This year, as of 30 September 2026, International Protection Appeal Tribunal (IPAT) has already closed 6,898 appeals exceeding the number of total appeals completed in 2025.
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 (IP Act 2026) gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable, and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether the Government remains committed to implementing the multi-agency competent authority model for the national referral mechanism established under the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Human Trafficking) Act 2024; and if not, the reasons for that decision.
reply:
The Government remains committed to strengthening the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), including through the expansion of the multi-agency competent authority model, and to ensuring that victims of human trafficking are identified and referred to appropriate supports as effectively and as early as possible. The NRM already operates on a multi-agency basis, with Departments, State agencies and other organisations identifying and referring potential victims. Under the current arrangements, An Garda Síochána is responsible for the formal identification of victims.
Part 3 of the Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Human Trafficking) Act 2024 provides for the formal identification function to be extended beyond An Garda Síochána to other designated bodies. Detailed implementation planning has identified practical and operational issues concerning the implementation and sequencing of these arrangements, including their interaction with broader State structures and processes. There is also a need to ensure appropriate alignment with changes across the migration and international protection systems.
In light of these issues, a phased approach is being taken to assigning formal identification responsibilities to the additional competent authorities on an administrative basis, while referral procedures related to the existing NRM are strengthened and the designated bodies put in place the necessary operational arrangements.
In parallel, my Department continues to progress wider reforms

question: Deputy James Geoghegan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide an update on the expansion of youth justice and youth diversion measures.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 44 and 75 together.
The Government’s approach to tackling youth offending is primarily through youth diversion and early intervention. The core exchequer and dormant account funding allocation for youth justice measures has almost doubled since 2020, standing at a record €43 million.
The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken. It follow operates a graduated response, ranging from diversion to detention. As offending increases in severity, so too does the criminal justice response to address youth crime.
The Government has fulfilled its commitment in the Youth Justice Strategy to ensure the availability of YDPs throughout the State. Every young person in Ireland now has access to a youth diversion service.
An evaluation of the YDPs was commissioned in 2022 and published in June 2023 concluding that YDPs are performing well in many areas that are known to impact positively on reducing crime and reoffending.
There has been an estimated 20% reduction in youth offences referred to An Garda Síochána between 2020 and 2025; with this decrease taking place during a period of population growth in the 12-17 cohort. question: Deputy Paula Butterly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he will provide an update on the progress of sentencing reform legislation contained in the programme for Government.
reply:
In January 2026, I secured cabinet approval for the drafting of a Judicial Council (Amendment Bill) and to publish the General Scheme. As the Deputy will be aware, the Judicial Council was established in 2019 to promote judicial independence as well as to ensure public confidence in the administration of justice. The Council is an independent body whose members are all of the judges in Ireland.
A key aim of the Bill is to ensure that the process for the adoption of Personal Injuries Guidelines is more transparent and comprehensive. It provides for a mechanism for the Judicial Council to reconsider revised Personal Injuries Guidelines, should the Oireachtas not approve the Guidelines presented to them. The Bill’s provisions in this regard also include procedural amendments regarding Sentencing Guidelines to align with the Supreme Court judgement in the Delaney case.
The General Scheme also provides for the Programme for Government commitment to empower the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration to ask the Judicial Council to draw up sentencing guidelines for a particular crime area, within a certain timeframe. It also requires the Council to comply with such a request.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration his plans to reform the operation of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings.
reply:
Ensuring transparency and promoting a greater understanding of the family law system is critical to maintaining and building trust in it. At the same time, those who seek the assistance of the courts in resolving their family justice disputes need to be assured that their privacy, and that of their children, will be maintained at what can be a very difficult time. In recognising the need for a balance between these two positions, the Family Justice Strategy commits to undertaking a review of the operation of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings.
Further to this commitment, an independent research report, entitled The Operation of the In Camera Rule in Family Law Proceedings, was published in 2025. The extensive report contains 21 detailed recommendations. Officials from my Department are currently considering the findings and recommendations of the report in the context of developing policy proposals for reform. Officials are also examining how family court proceedings operate in other jurisdictions, to see what can be learned from them.
Following on from the findings of the report, I commissioned the Child Law Project to deliver the Family Law Reporting Project. The first volume of case reports was published by my Department on the 19 August 2026. reply:
CCTV in public places has a role in giving people a greater sense of security. Whilst the use of CCTV by An Garda Síochána and Local Authorities can have great merit, its use can have a direct impact on the human rights of individuals. Therefore, its installation and operation must be carefully planned and its use competently managed, ensuring compliance with data protection law and regulations.
The Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) Act 2023 was enacted on 5 December 2023. Part 5 of the Act, which relates to public CCTV, was not commenced at that time as it required the completion of operational guidelines and further legislative changes. The enactment of the Garda Síochána (Recording Devices) (Amendment) Act 2026 in July 2026 and the recent completion of the Garda CCTV Code of Practice means that Part 5 of the Act will be commenced in the coming weeks.
The commencement of Part 5 will establish a new statutory framework for the authorisation and operation of public CCTV schemes, repealing Section 38 of the Garda Síochána Act 2005.

question: Deputy Matt Carthy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if his Department has examined the impact on the administration of justice of the reduction in the number of criminal legal aid certificates granted since 1 July 2026.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 33 and 70 together.
The reform of the criminal legal aid fee structure in the District Court is designed to improve efficiencies, reduce unnecessary adjournments, simplify the administration of criminal legal aid, speed up case resolution and enable faster payments to practitioners through the repeal of previous regulations and the provision of new regulatory arrangements.
Since the commencement of the new system, and as of 2 October, almost 2,400 new certificates (invoices for payment) for legal aid have issued with an approximate total value of €1.25 million in the District Court alone.
It should be noted that, under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. My Department has no involvement in the granting of free legal aid or the assignment of solicitors. These matters are handled entirely by the courts. Under the Courts Service Act 1998, the management and administration of the courts is a matter for the Courts Service, while the allocation of court business, the scheduling of cases and the management of court lists are matters for the Judiciary, in particular the Presidents of the Courts.

question: Deputy Grace Boland asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the measures being taken to support and expand youth justice and diversion initiatives aimed at preventing young people from becoming involved in criminal activity; the level of funding provided for such initiatives in each of the past three years and planned for 2027; and the metrics used to assess their effectiveness and outcome.

The Youth Justice Strategy 2021-2027 emphasises early intervention, prevention, family support and community engagement. It targets behavioural change so the cycle of offending by young people is broken.

Youth Diversion Projects (YDPs) are community-based, multi-agency youth crime prevention initiatives which primarily seek to divert young people who have been, or are at risk of becoming, involved in anti-social and/or criminal behaviour away from formal engagement with the Criminal Justice System. There are currently 92 YDPs and 4 Targeted Youth Diversion Projects in operation nationwide. In 2025 these youth diversion projects and targeted youth diversion projects engaged with 4,786 young persons.

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of persons diverted by An Garda Síochána to health services under the health diversion scheme since its commencement; the number of Garda members who received specific training on the operation of the scheme prior to its commencement and to date; and the number of occasions on which a person eligible for diversion was not referred.
reply:
The Health Referral Scheme is a health-led response for people who are found in possession of drugs for personal use for the first time. The scheme provides eligible adults with an opportunity to engage with health services at an early stage, receive advice and support and, where appropriate, be referred to further services.
The scheme is now live nationally and is supported by investment in HSE services across all health regions.
The scheme does not legalise drug use but has been introduced as a health-led pathway for eligible first-time personal possession cases, with a focus on early intervention, reducing harm and supporting people to access appropriate services.
All first-time drug offenders must be assessed for suitability for the scheme by the investigating Garda member, in consultation with their Superintendent or an Inspector acting in that capacity. Where a decision is made not to offer a health referral, the rationale for that decision must be clearly recorded and communicated to the person concerned.
It should be noted that the scheme is voluntary. If the person is eligible and consents to partake in the scheme they are referred to the HSE for support. Those referred will receive information and advice on reducing harm and if additional support is needed, the person may be referred to addiction or other health services.
As the scheme has only recently been implemented, the specific data on the numbers referred or partaking in the scheme are not available.

question: Deputy Cathal Crowe asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if consideration has been given to the policy of introducing a personal tax credit for people with a disability in employment.
reply:
The Government recognises the significant financial pressures experienced by households with disabilities, particularly amid the heightened cost?of?living conditions of recent years. In response, we have implemented targeted budget measures designed to support those most vulnerable.
When this Government took office, we committed to a step change in the delivery of supports and services for people with disability and their families, in line with our Programme for Government commitments.
There are currently a number of tax measures within the tax system that support people with disabilities and carers, this includes Tax Relief for Health Expenses which provides relief to individuals who have incurred costs in respect of qualifying health expenses and the Blind Person’s Tax Credit, which is available to a blind person or a person who has impaired vision.
There are more than 346,000 people with disabilities in Ireland who are already in work. They are contributing to our economy, supporting their families and communities, and making an enormous contribution to our country.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance the number of individual taxpayers who have paid tax as a result of the so-called "deemed disposal" rule in relation to exchange traded funds in each year since it was introduced; and the total tax revenue generated in each year.
reply:
The information available to Revenue does not allow them to isolate the tax returned due to the deemed disposal rule from other chargeable events which give rise to a tax liability. Chargeable events include:
• the making of relevant payments;
• the redemption of the investment;
• the transfer by an investor of their investment; and
• the ending of an eight-year period following the acquisition of the investment and then every eight years thereafter (deemed disposal).
Therefore, it is not possible to directly identify the tax revenue arising from the application of the deemed disposal rule. This is because investment funds and life companies are not obliged to report the category of chargeable event that the exit tax relates to at the time of making payment to Revenue. Similarly, as respects investments in certain Irish domiciled funds and offshore funds in respect of which investors are required to self-assess tax due, taxpayers are not required to separately report data for each category of chargeable event when filing their tax return.

question: Deputy Peter 'Chap' Cleere asked the Tánaiste and Minister for Finance if he will clarify whether new tax exemptions or incentives that are being introduced to encourage personal savings and investment will also apply to individuals who have already established savings or investment policies; if existing investments will be eligible for the same tax treatment as new investments.
reply:
Encouraging retail investment remains a key priority of mine. As the Deputy is aware, Budget 2026 included a commitment to publish a Roadmap: ‘Taxation of Retail Investment – A New Path Forward for Ireland’, setting out the intended approach to simplify and adapt the tax framework to encourage retail investment while retaining necessary and important anti-avoidance protections, in a proportionate manner.
The Roadmap was published on 31 August.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Transport If his attention has been drawn to the actions of the French government which has introduced a specific penalty of €100 per tonne for non-compliance with CORSIA offsetting obligations together with the possibility of an operating ban; whether the Government will introduce an equivalent national penalty for non-compliance with CORSIA that is consistent with the excess emissions penalty applicable under the EU ETS, in order to ensure that Irish airlines operate on a level playing field with competitors in other Member States and to support the integrity of multilateral climate action.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92 and 93 together.
The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) was adopted by ICAO in 2016 as a global market-based measure to address CO? emissions from international aviation. The scheme requires airlines to offset emissions above an agreed baseline and is being implemented in three phases: a Pilot Phase (2021-2023), Phase I (2024-2026) and Phase II (2027-2035). Participation is voluntary during the first two phases, while from 2027 the scheme will apply more broadly, subject to certain exemptions, including for Least Developed Countries, Small Island Developing States and Landlocked Developing Countries. Ireland, together with all EU Member States, has participated in CORSIA since its commencement. Participation has continued to expand, with 130 States participating in the scheme from 1 January 2026.
CORSIA enters Phase II from 1 January 2027 during which participation will be determined based on 2018 Revenue Tonne Kilometres (RTK) data. As a result, participation is anticipated to expand further to 134 States as Brazil, China, India and the Russian Federation will come into scope for participation.
Within the EU, both CORSIA and the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) are implemented through Directive 2003/87/EC. reply:

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Transport the measures in place to ensure quicker recognition of driving licences of bus and truck drivers from outside the European economic area.
reply:
The exchange of non-EU driving licences is managed through the National Driver Licence Service, the provision of which is delegated under national legislation to the Road Safety Authority. The requirements of the licensing process, including licence exchange, are available on www.ndls.ie.
There are various factors which can affect the time it takes to process licence exchange applications. For example, the applicant may need to submit outstanding information, such as a medical or eyesight report, or the physical driving licence itself in the case of an online application.
The most common reason for delays is in verification of the driving licence by the other licensing authority. However, it is vital, to protect the safety of Irish road users and the integrity of the Irish licensing system, that the validity of a driving licence presented for exchange can be verified.
Neither I nor my officials have any role in the exchange application process. Therefore, I have therefore referred your query regarding the exchange of bus and truck licences to the Authority for direct reply. Please contact my office if a response is not provided within 10 working days.

question: Deputy John McGuinness asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht if the financial support given to volunteer centres relative to their work in the area of integration, will be continued and increased in Budget 2027.
reply:
The Department of Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht provides funding and other supports to the network of 29 Volunteer Centres across the country, as well as to a number of national volunteer-supporting organisations including Volunteer Ireland.
The Deputy can be reassured that the Department is committed to supporting communities, including supporting volunteering in our communities. Funding for Volunteer Centres, as well as for national volunteer-supporting organisations and the wider community and voluntary sector, in 2027 will be considered as part of the Government’s usual Budgetary processes.

question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the reason grants for Men’s Sheds are not proceeding in 2026; if he will reconsider the decision in view of the important role Men’s Sheds play across communities; details of other funding streams available to Men's Sheds.
reply:
My Department is very supportive of both Men’s Sheds and Women’s Sheds. Indeed, I can assure the Deputy that I am very conscious of the important role that these groups play in communities across the country. Men’s Sheds provide a space for men of all ages to come together on a regular basis in a safe, comfortable and inclusive environment.
My Department provides funding to Men’s Sheds under various funding supports, including:
• The Local Enhancement Programme (LEP);
• The Social Inclusion and Community Activation Programme (SICAP) 2024 - 2028; and
• The LEADER programme.
Since 2018, under my Department’s Local Enhancement Programme (LEP) and its iterations, Men’s Sheds have been allocated over €2.7 million, to assist with building upgrades and the purchase of equipment.
My Department also provides funding directly to the Irish Men's Shed Association (IMSA) under the Scheme to Support National Organisations (SSNO). The SSNO provides multi-annual funding towards core costs of national, community and voluntary organisations. The current iteration of the SSNO commenced on 1 July 2026, with funding of €297,766 over the three-years and 6-month period being provided to the IMSA.
In addition, since 2022, my Department has also provided over €2.3 million in current funding directly to the IMSA for onward distribution to individual Men's Sheds. Following a recent meeting with the IMSA to discuss this funding I received a new proposal in relation to the distribution of the funding.

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Rural and Community Development and the Gaeltacht the amount of ORIS funding that has been allocated to Tipperary County Council for each of the years 2022 to 2025 and to date in 2026, in tabular form.
reply:
The Outdoor Recreation Infrastructure Scheme (ORIS) provides funding under several measures for the development of new outdoor recreational infrastructure and for the necessary repair, enhancement or promotion of existing outdoor recreation infrastructure in countryside areas across Ireland. The deadline for applications for smaller projects under measure 1 and the project development measure has now passed and my officials are reviewing these applications.

question: Deputy Eoghan Kenny asked the Minister for Transport if the reliability of the morning bus service in Whitechurch is being formally monitored by the relevant transport authority.
reply:

We are at a key juncture for public transport in Ireland. Reliable and sustainable services are critical as passenger numbers grow, congestion worsens in urban areas, and a greater proportion of the population depends on public transport for commuting, education, and essential travel.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if the impact of these transport challenges on student participation, retention and educational opportunity has been assessed; the measures being considered to support affected students.
reply:
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026–2035, published in March of this year, recognises the relationship between accommodation availability and student commuting patterns.
The Strategy highlights the need to address long and unsustainable student commutes through greater integration of accommodation, transport planning and sustainable mobility initiatives. It recognises that excessive commuting can create barriers to accessing and participating in higher education and sets out measures to better understand and address these challenges through improved data collection, coordinated planning and cross-sectoral collaboration.
In particular, the Strategy includes commitments to support higher education institutions (HEIs) in developing sustainable commuting policies, improving understanding of student travel behaviours and strengthening engagement with relevant transport stakeholders. HEIs are encouraged to use data-driven insights to assess student mobility needs and support more efficient and sustainable commuting, while participating in sustainable transport initiatives and promoting active travel and public transport options.
The Strategy also provides for a pilot programme aimed at strengthening collaboration between HEIs, the National Transport Authority (NTA), local authorities and transport operators. question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the progress that has been made in acquiring lands for a third level institution in Swords County Dublin; if a site has been identified and purchased; and the exact location.
reply:
Dublin and Dún Laoghaire ETB (DDLETB) are currently being supported by SOLAS in developing their Preliminary Business Case for their proposal under the FET College Major Capital Programme.
The site preference for this new college is Swords due to its population base and future growth projections. A site option was previously identified but unfortunately despite the best efforts of DDLETB, they were not able to complete the legal and site due diligence on the site due to a number of issues remaining outstanding including access and site boundaries.
I understand that DDLETB are currently working closely with the Local Authority towards the identification of other sites in the Swords area, suitable for this FET College. A meeting is being arranged this week between my officials, the Local Authority and DDLETB to progress this.
SOLAS and my department will endeavour to continue to support DDLETB in progressing this major capital project which will deliver key FET infrastructure to meet the needs of learners in Fingal and surrounding areas.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science to provide funding for public owned college student accommodation in Tralee, County Kerry, given that currently all student beds in Tralee are privately owned.
reply:
The Government recognises the importance of ensuring an adequate supply of affordable and sustainable student accommodation across all regions, including Tralee, County Kerry.
The National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026–2035, published in March 2026, provides the framework for increasing student accommodation capacity, improving affordability and supporting the long-term delivery of student accommodation nationwide. The Strategy notes that lessons were learned following a Short-Term Activation Programme, which provided Government funding to assist in the delivery of around 1,000 new PBSA beds., namely that the cost per bed under the programme indicated a funding level that would be untenable for the State, given the projected requirement of 42,000 addition student beds by 2035.
A key initiative under the Student Accommodation Strategy is the Higher Education Institution Student Accommodation Programme (HSAP), which is being advanced by my Department in partnership with the Higher Education Authority and the National Development Finance Agency. The programme will assist HEIs in securing additional Purpose-Built Student Accommodation (PBSA) capacity, through private development, delivering accommodation on or near campus via nomination agreements, licensed sites, and site servicing arrangements.

question: Deputy Brian Brennan asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science if his attention has been drawn to the ongoing delays in registration of students at Technological University Dublin following on from issues with result delays earlier this year; and the action that has been taken to resolve this issue.
reply:
Thank you, Deputy, for your question.
I am aware of issues raised earlier this academic year regarding the publication of some examination results and the associated timing of registration for certain students at Technological University Dublin (TU Dublin). However, at this point in time I understand that those issues have been resolved.
As the Deputy will no doubt be aware, TU Dublin is an autonomous higher education institution under the Technological Universities Act 2018 and, as such, is responsible for the management of its academic and administrative affairs, including student registration and the administration of examinations.
Nevertheless, my officials have engaged with the HEA to seek updates from TU Dublin in relation to these matters.
As of 18th September, TU Dublin confirmed 93% of the overall student cohort had been issued an invitation to register (ITR). The University also clarified that students who have not yet received an ITR continue to have full access to the University’s facilities and resources while awaiting the completion of the relevant results and registration processes. Arrangements were also in place to facilitate access to learning materials for students awaiting registration.
My understanding is that registration processes are operating as planned and that students are being registered in line with normal University procedures.

question: Deputy Ivana Bacik asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science the measures his Department is taking to address the growing affordability crisis facing students in third-level education, particularly in relation to the escalating cost of student accommodation; and the measures his Department intends to make to ensure that young people can access and fully participate in higher education regardless of their financial circumstances.
reply:
I am very mindful of the financial pressures facing students and families, particularly the cost of student accommodation. To inform Budget 2027, I recently published the Annual Options Paper on Reducing the Cost of Education, setting out a range of measures for consideration to reduce costs and provide greater certainty for students and their families.
In March 2026, I published the National Student Accommodation Strategy 2026-2035, which sets out a pathway to improve access to higher education by addressing accommodation affordability and supply and viability.
My Department, with the support of the HEA and the NDFA, is progressing the Higher Education Institution Student Accommodation Programme. This programme will support the delivery of additional purpose-built student accommodation through partnerships with higher education institutions and the private sector, including nomination agreements, licensed sites and site-servicing arrangements.
The Strategy also builds on the Short-Term Activation Programme, under which almost 1,000 beds have been delivered or are being progressed, with 30% provided at discounted rents. In addition, the strategy contains measures to expand Rent-a-Room provision.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Further and Higher Education, Research, Innovation and Science his plans to increase the support for dyslexic students in third level education.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 728, 729 and 730 together.
Under the National Access Plan (NAP) 2022-2028 inclusion and diversity in the student body in Higher Education is a key priority.
The Plan has identified a number of priority-groups who continue to be underrepresented in higher education including students with disabilities.
The Programme for Access to Higher Education (PATH) is the main funding stream that supports the implementation of the NAP. PATH is delivered through five strands that work together to widen participation and support student success, with PATH 4 targeting those with disabilities.
Targets in the NAP for new entrant students with a disability are set at 16% by 2028, and we have reached this at the midterm point of the plan with current figures at 16.3%.
The main source of funding for Students with disabilities is the Fund for Students with Disabilities (FSD) which allocates funding to HEIs for the provision of services and supports to full- and part-time students with disabilities. The FSD provides supports for students with dyslexia, autism and mild general learning difficulties among a wide range of disabilities which are supported by the fund.
The FSD aims to ensure that students with disabilities have the necessary supports and equipment to enable them to access, fully participate in and successfully complete their chosen course of study. In Budget 2026 I increased funding by €1m bringing the total annual fund in higher education to over €10.5m

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health whether the free HRT scheme will be extended to cover hormone replacement therapy for patients with congenital or permanent endocrine conditions, including testosterone replacement for Klinefelter syndrome.
reply:
The HSE has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. This arises from the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
Reimbursement is for licenced indications which have been granted marketing authorisation by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA). Pharmaceutical companies must apply to the HSE for reimbursement.
Under the Free Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) arrangement, which came into effect on 1 June 2025, where a woman has been prescribed a HRT product on the reimbursement list by her healthcare provider for the purpose of alleviating the symptoms associated with all stages of menopause, the cost of the HRT medications or products, and the dispensing fees will be met by the State.
This measure is intended to support the management of the symptoms of menopause and, therefore, relates to the provision of treatment for a specific medical condition/life stage i.e. menopause. HRT is the most commonly used treatment for managing symptoms of menopause and has shown to be the most effective intervention.
Menopause has been highlighted as a key priority area by the Women’s Health Taskforce. It is a key action in the Women’s Health Action Plans. A number of measures have been implemented in recent years to improve the experience of menopause for women in Ireland, including this HRT arrangement.
HRT is used in the treatment of other medical conditions, including gender-affirm

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Health the action the HSE and HPRA are taking on the current supply shortage of budesonide orodispersible tablets in the State.
reply:
The Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA), as the competent authority in Ireland for coordinating the management of medicine shortages, has advised that it has received no notifications indicating a current supply interruption affecting Jorveza (budesonide orodispersible tablets).
Ireland has a multi-stakeholder Medicines Shortages Framework, operated by the HPRA, through which the Department of Health, the Health Service Executive (HSE), the HPRA and other stakeholders work together to help prevent and mitigate medicine shortages and minimise any impact on patients.
Marketing authorisation holders are required to report actual and anticipated medicine shortages to the HPRA. Where a shortage is reported, details are assessed by the HPRA and published on its publicly available medicines shortages database.
Patients who are experiencing difficulty obtaining their medication should consult their healthcare professional, such as their GP or pharmacist.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 603 and 695 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy and is built around the principle of woman-centred care.
Care is delivered through three pathways, tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:
- The Supported Care Pathway – for normal-risk pregnancies, led by midwives within a multidisciplinary team.
- The Assisted Care Pathway – for medium-risk pregnancies, or normal-risk pregnancies where obstetric care is chosen.
- The Specialised Care Pathway – for high-risk pregnancies, led by a named consultant obstetrician with midwives and other specialists.
Women are offered a choice of pathways, with a focus on the normalisation of pregnancy and birth, continuity of care, and one-to-one support in labour.
While women’s choice is facilitated wherever possible as patient safety takes priority in the delivery of services.
The DOMINO Scheme is a highly valued scheme offering a midwifery-led model of care for women on the supported care pathway with uncomplicated pregnancies. question: Deputy Mary Lou McDonald asked the Minister for Health the measures being taken to reduce waiting times for endometriosis assessment and specialist treatment in Ireland.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 686, 687 and 688 together.
On 18 October 2025, I launched the National Framework for the Management of Endometriosis. The Framework sets out for the first time in Ireland a defined clinical pathway for women with endometriosis, which spans primary to secondary care to specialist complex care in tertiary settings.
Developed by the HSE's National Women and Infants Health Programme (NWIHP), the Framework marks the first step in developing a more holistic and comprehensive approach to care for women with endometriosis in Ireland.
Central to the Model of Care is the principle of presumed diagnosis, acknowledging that women are always the most reliable narrators of their own symptoms and pain. The Framework reflects the voices of patient advocates and aims to transform how endometriosis is recognised and treated across the country.
Regional Specialist Centres for moderate cases have been established in the Rotunda Hospital, the Coombe Hospital, and University Hospital Limerick, with clinics under further development in University Hospital Galway and the National Maternity Hospital.
Two supra-regional specialist centres, in Tallaght University Hospital and Cork University Maternity Hospital, have been established for the management of complex cases.

question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Health if her Department is considering measures aimed at reducing the financial burden on coeliac sufferers who must abide by a gluten free diet.
reply:
The Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines and medical items, in accordance with the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013.
In line with the 2013 Act and the national framework agreed with industry, a company must submit an application to the HSE to have a new medicine added to the formal Reimbursement list. In making a relevant reimbursement decision, the HSE is required under the Act to have regard to a number of criteria including efficacy, the health needs of the public, cost effectiveness and potential or actual budget impact.
Gluten-free products were removed from the list of reimbursable items under the General Medical Services (GMS) scheme, with several other products, in September 2012. The marketplace has evolved whereby such products are widely available in supermarkets at a more reasonable price than was historically costed to the State when they were available in pharmacies through the statutory schemes, and without incurring the further extra costs of a dispensing fee. There are currently no plans to reinstate these products on the list of reimbursable items under the GMS and other community drug schemes.
Patients can claim tax relief for certain food products if they have specific dietary requirements due to a medical condition. This applies to persons with coeliac disease where they require gluten free foods specifically manufactured to be gluten free.

Ireland is among the highest spenders on health across the EU (OECD), with the third-highest rate of State coverage of pharmaceutical expenditure in Europe.
In line with the commitments set out in the Programme for Government, the Government will continue to prioritise improving the affordability of healthcare and medicines, including through ongoing review of community drugs schemes such as the Drugs Payment Scheme (DPS).

question: Deputy Cathy Bennett asked the Minister for Health the advice that she can provide to a person (details supplied) resident in Monaghan who has contacted every GP in the county and has been unable to register with a GP for them and their child.
reply:
GPs are private practitioners, most of whom hold a GMS contract with the HSE for the provision of GP services without charge to medical card and GP visit card holders. Eligibility for a medical card, or a GP visit card for those aged between 8 and 69 years of age, is primarily based on means testing. All children under 8 years of age and all those aged 70 years and over are eligible for a GP visit card.
Where a person that holds a medical card or GP visit card, or a person eligible for either card, experiences difficulty in finding a GP to accept them as a patient, the person concerned having unsuccessfully applied to at least three GPs in the area (or fewer if there are fewer GPs in the area) can apply to the HSE Eligibility Unit which has the power to assign a GMS patient to a GP's GMS patient list, in accordance with the GMS contract. People who do not hold a medical card or GP visit card access GP services on a private basis and can make enquiries directly to any GP practice they wish to register with. As private practitioners, it is a matter for each individual GP to decide whether to accept additional private patients.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Health the total capital expenditure incurred by the HSE and her Department on the development of day-surgery centres and elective hospitals in each year from 2020 to date, by site; the estimated final project cost for each completed, active and planned facility; and the expected opening date of each facility.
reply:
Since its approval by Government in December 2021, the Elective Ambulatory Care Programme has been evolving to ensure that medium term demand and capacity for elective day-case care can be met through the delivery of a national network of nine Surgical Hubs in the first instance, while also planning for future elective care capacity requirements through a national network of Elective Treatment Centres (ETCs), also known as Elective Hospitals, in Cork, Galway and Dublin.
Four Surgical Hubs are now operational in Tallaght (the Reeves Centre), South Dublin (Mt Carmel), North Dublin (Swords) and Cork, with Hubs at Waterford, Limerick and Galway due to open in the coming months. Plans are also advancing for Surgical Hubs in Sligo and Letterkenny. Together these nine Hubs will provide significant additional elective care capacity across the country, including 30 day-case theatres, 16 minor operations theatres, and 38 outpatient diagnostic/treatment rooms, and will help drive down waiting times for elective day-case care.
The Elective Treatment Centres, also known as Elective Hospitals, are being developed to meet the longer term elective care needs of the country. Locations identified are in Cork (at St Stephen’s Hospital, Glanmire), Galway (Merlin Park) and Dublin (emerging preferred sites previously identified at Connolly Hospital in Blanchardstown and at Crumlin-Children’s Health Ireland). The HSE is continuing to progress the detailed design works for the ETCs in Cork and Galwa

question: Deputy Louis O'Hara asked the Minister for Health if her Department is working to develop access to a medical device for Irish patients (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 595 and 664 together.
For a product to be considered for addition to the Reimbursement List, the company must submit a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013. To date, an application has not been made for Omnipod® 5 by the company to the HSE.
Clinical and cost-effectiveness assessments are carried out after a company submits a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE. As such no such assessment has been carried out.
The HSE has advised that the company has not yet launched the product to the Irish market. Omnipod® 5 is being rolled out world-wide on a phased basis due to constraints in manufacturing capacity versus demand and the company informed the HSE that they do not yet have a timeline for launch in Ireland.
On the 21st of May, The Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care was launched by the Minister for Health.
This is Ireland’s first national strategy for diabetes. It sets out recommendations for action in relation to type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, diabetes in pregnancy and paediatric diabetes. The strategy marks a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland, representing the development of a unified approach to the delivery of diabetes care.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Transport if he is satisfied that the regulatory framework governing the SPSV sector is being determined by the National Transport Authority in the public interest rather than being shaped by the corporate structures and business models of large international platform operators.
reply:

question: Deputy Mark Ward asked the Minister for Health if the MCAP review has commenced; if stakeholders have been appointed to the review group; and the length of time the review is expected to take once it begins.
reply:
On 1st April 2026, Minister for Health Jennifer Carroll MacNeill formally appointed Professor Shane Allwright to chair the Review Group.
The Group will:
- Review the current operation of the Medical Cannabis Access Programme and the availability of Schedule 2 Cannabis products.
- Examine the appropriateness to expand the range of conditions covered by the programme, where sufficient evidence exists that cannabis may prove beneficial.
- Review the current access to Schedule 1 Cannabis products and the current operation of the ministerial licence.
- Develop a national policy on access to, and the administration of cannabis products that are subject to ministerial licence.
The Review Group is comprised of a wide range of medical specialists and experts including patient representatives.
The timeline for completing the “Review of Access to Cannabis for Medical Use” which also evaluates the Medical Cannabis Access Programme (MCAP) is anticipated to be in the region of 12 months from the date of the group's initial meeting which took place on 27th May 2026.

question: Deputy Pádraig O'Sullivan asked the Minister for Health the way in which the suspension of the DOMINO scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital is consistent with the supported care pathway under the National Maternity Strategy 2016–2026; and whether the successor to that strategy will commit to protecting and expanding midwife-led continuity of care schemes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 603 and 695 together.
Maternity care in Ireland is provided in line with the National Maternity Strategy and is built around the principle of woman-centred care.
Care is delivered through three pathways, tailored to the clinical needs and risk profile of each woman and her baby:
- The Supported Care Pathway – for normal-risk pregnancies, led by midwives within a multidisciplinary team.
- The Assisted Care Pathway – for medium-risk pregnancies, or normal-risk pregnancies where obstetric care is chosen.
- The Specialised Care Pathway – for high-risk pregnancies, led by a named consultant obstetrician with midwives and other specialists.
Women are offered a choice of pathways, with a focus on the normalisation of pregnancy and birth, continuity of care, and one-to-one support in labour.
While women’s choice is facilitated wherever possible as patient safety takes priority in the delivery of services.
The DOMINO Scheme is a highly valued scheme offering a midwifery-led model of care for women on the supported care pathway with uncomplicated pregnancies. The DOMINO Scheme at Cork University Maternity Hospital remains operational and available both to women currently using the service and to new patients who meet the eligibility criteria. I understand the concern arising from recent reports of changes to the operation of the Scheme in Cork. question: Deputy Séamus McGrath asked the Minister for Health if she will give consideration to approving an insulin pump (details supplied) for a patient with Type 1 diabetes.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 595 and 664 together.
For a product to be considered for addition to the Reimbursement List, the company must submit a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013. To date, an application has not been made for Omnipod® 5 by the company to the HSE.
Clinical and cost-effectiveness assessments are carried out after a company submits a pricing and reimbursement application to the HSE. As such no such assessment has been carried out.
The HSE has advised that the company has not yet launched the product to the Irish market. Omnipod® 5 is being rolled out world-wide on a phased basis due to constraints in manufacturing capacity versus demand and the company informed the HSE that they do not yet have a timeline for launch in Ireland.
On the 21st of May, The Diabetes Policy and Services Review: A Strategy for Better Care was launched by the Minister for Health.
This is Ireland’s first national strategy for diabetes. It sets out recommendations for action in relation to type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, diabetes in pregnancy and paediatric diabetes. The strategy marks a major milestone in diabetes care in Ireland, representing the development of a unified approach to the delivery of diabetes care.

question: Deputy Noel McCarthy asked the Minister for Health to outline the measures being taken to reduce delays in the repayment of applications under the Cross Border Directive.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 544 and 594 together.
The Cross Border Directive allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the cross-border directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.
The continued growth in use of the scheme has placed additional demands on the HSE CBD office and given rise to a build-up of applications. The increased activity is evidenced by the number of treatments reimbursed increasing by approx. 75% between 2020 and 2024.
It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently (as of 2 September 2026) processing applications received at the end of February 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Health for an update on the proposed prohibition on the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children under 16 years of age.
reply:
Stimulant drinks, commonly known as energy drinks, are often marketed as products that improve energy, focus and performance. However, many contain high levels of caffeine and sugar and may have negative effects on health, particularly for children and young people.
In September 2026, Safefood published its report, A survey of energy drinks on the island of Ireland 2026. The report found high levels of energy drink consumption among young people, with more than half of 15 to 24-year-olds reporting that they consume energy drinks at least once a week. The report also found strong public support for restrictions on the sale of energy drinks to children, with more than three-quarters of adults supporting the introduction of a legal age restriction.
The Government recognises the public health concerns associated with the consumption of high-caffeine energy drinks by children and young people. The Department of Health is considering the findings of the Safefood report and other available evidence in relation to possible measures to reduce children's access to these products. This issue is also being considered in the context of the forthcoming Obesity Policy and Action Plan and its focus on creating healthier food environments and supporting healthier choices for children and young people.
Any proposal to introduce restrictions on the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks would require careful consideration of the public health benefits, regulatory implications and enforcement arran

question: Deputy Marie Sherlock asked the Minister for Health the current status of the Rotunda Maternity Hospital capital project; and the timeline for progressing this project.
reply:
This Government is committed to driving improvements across maternity services including continued investment in the Rotunda Hospital, Dublin.
The Minister for Health was deeply disappointed by the decision of An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to overturn the position of Dublin City Council and refuse planning permission for the proposed Critical Care Wing at the Rotunda.
The planned development at Parnell Square West is necessary to provide essential upgrades to the Rotunda that are needed now and includes capital developments to manage the current and future needs of women and babies.
The Minister met with the Master of the Rotunda and agreed that a new planning application will be submitted by the Rotunda.
The application will also include critical care capacity for women, expanding on the earlier application, which was focused solely on infants, and will also include provision for an enhanced Sexual Assault Treatment Unit.
The Rotunda and HSE are preparing a pre-application submission which will facilitate the direct application of planning permission to ACP. This process is in line with the requirements of the Planning and Development Act 2000.
The Minister’s priority is to ensure the delivery of appropriate neonatal and critical care capacity for the Rotunda as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy John Brady asked the Minister for Health to provide an update on plans to make the shingles vaccine free for people aged over 65.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 546 and 583 together.
The immunisation programme in Ireland is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
The Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) has carried out a Health Technology Assessment (HTA) on the herpes zoster vaccine which protects against shingles. A HTA is a multidisciplinary research process that collects and summarises information about a health technology. HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.
HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

reply:
The Government is committed to investing in new medicines. Supported by €158 million of funding in Budgets 2021-2025, the State delivered access to 250 new medicines. 70 of these were for rare diseases. Budget 2026 allocated €217 million additional investment in medicines, including €30 million in funding for new medicines. This has, as of August 2026, delivered access to 30 new medicines, including 7 for rare diseases.
The Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on pricing and reimbursement of medicines, in accordance with the provisions of the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013. The Minister has no role in decisions on pricing and reimbursement.
The HSE robustly assesses applications for pricing and reimbursement to make sure that it can stretch available resources as far as possible and to deliver the best value in relation to each medicine and ultimately more medicines to Irish citizens and patients.
There are formal processes which govern applications for the pricing and reimbursement of medicines, and new uses of existing medicines, to be funded and / or reimbursed. HSE decisions on which medicines are reimbursed by the taxpayer are made on objective, scientific and economic grounds.

question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Health if the recruitment freeze in Galway University hospital will be lifted in order to fill the 23 vacant midwifery posts; and the way in which she plans to retain recently qualified midwives in Ireland while a recruitment ban is in place.
reply:
There is no recruitment embargo in place in the HSE. However, due to ongoing budgetary issues, several Regional Health Authorities (RHA) have been placed in a strengthened financial control framework. One of these is the West & North-West RHA, which includes Galway University Hospital.
In the period from 1 January 2026 to 31 August 2026, the West & North-West RHA incurred pay costs of €1,286 million against a budget of €1,254 million, equating to a deficit of €32 million (2.6%). To manage these costs, the HSE placed the West & North-West RHA in a strengthened financial control framework, one of whose measures is a requirement for HSE CEO approval of any proposed recruitment. A further requirement for Departmental sanction of any recruitment proposals was announced in recent weeks.
These controls are about ensuring that new recruitment is properly prioritised, affordable, evidenced and clearly linked to patient need. The HSE must show that the need and any patient-safety risk have been assessed, that alternatives such as redeployment, roster changes, skill-mix changes, staff banks, agency conversion, cross-site working or the use of vacancies have been considered, and that funding or a genuine recurring offset is available.
Any requests to recruit additional midwives to Galway University Hospital maternity services will be considered in this context.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Health her plans to increase education about HPV, and the vaccine in schools.
reply:
Increasing vaccination uptake rates in the routine HPV vaccination programme is vital in order for Ireland to achieve elimination of cervical cancer by its target date of 2040. The World Health Organisation has set a target for all countries to ensure that 90% of girls are vaccinated with the HPV vaccine by the age of 15 years.
The ages at which vaccines are recommended in the immunisation schedule are recommended by the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC), in order to give each child the best possible protection against vaccine preventable diseases. As the HPV vaccine is a preventative measure, it is intended to be administered, if possible, before a person becomes exposed to HPV infection. Therefore, the gender-neutral HPV vaccination programme targets all girls and boys in first year of secondary school.
The Laura Brennan HPV Catch-up Vaccination Programme offered HPV vaccination to 5th and 6th year students in secondary school for the 2025/2026 academic year, as a once off opportunity, for those who previously missed the HPV vaccine while in first year of secondary school.
The second phase of the programme launched on 3 September with HSE vaccination teams visiting post-primary schools across the country to offer the HPV vaccine to eligible students.
The programme is open to:
• All eligible boys and girls in 2nd to 5th year of post-primary (secondary) school.
• Home-educated young people born between 1 September 2008 and 31 August 2013.

The immunisation programme in Ireland is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.

HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.
HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

reply:
