The Cross Border Directive allows public patients to access necessary healthcare, which they would have been entitled to access in the public healthcare service in Ireland, in another EU or EEA country. The patient pays upfront for the treatment and is reimbursed upon return to Ireland.
The HSE is responsible for the operation of the cross-border directive and has a dedicated office for that purpose.

It is important that this service operates in a responsive way and that reimbursement applications are processed within a reasonable timeframe. The HSE advises it usually aims to repay patients within 30 working days of receipt of all completed documents. The HSE advise the CBD office is currently (as of 2 September 2026) processing applications received at the end of February 2026. A 6-month delay for reimbursement is clearly unacceptable. To address this the HSE has advised my Department that additional resources are being assigned to manage this increase in demand with the aim of restoring processing times to expected levels. I have set the HSE a specific target of getting back to the 30-day target by the end of 2026.

question: Deputy Richard Boyd Barrett asked the Minister for Transport if his attention has been drawn to the rising increase in driving test wait times as reported today (details supplied), particularly in Dún Laoghaire where wait times have risen again to 19 weeks this month and the impact this is having on those waiting for tests for employment/education and other reasons; if he will outline the immediate steps he is taking to bring down waiting times permanently; and if emergency slots have been considered for those who can provide supporting evidence of the necessity of an early test.

Under the Road Safety Authority Act 2006, the Road Safety Authority (RSA) has statutory responsibility for all aspects of the National Driver Testing Service.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality if she is familiar with the remit of the UK Office of Public Guardian; and which Irish statutory body performs the same or similar functions by investigating allegations of mistreatment of elderly people at the hands of family members who may have powers of attorney over their affairs.
reply:
In Ireland, under the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015 (2015 Act), the DSS has statutory responsibility for the review, registration and supervision of Enduring Powers of Attorney (EPA), including the investigation of complaints in relation to the execution of a person’s responsibilities as an attorney under the Act. Safeguarding of adults with decision-making difficulties is central to the EPA application and registration process under the 2015 Act.
As part of the registration process for an EPA, the DSS must review it with regard to the suitability of the attorney and its compliance with the 2015 Act. There are also notice periods set out in the 2015 Act which enable notice parties to object to the registration of the EPA on number of grounds, including, inter alia, that the donor did not have capacity, that fraud, coercion or undue influence was used to induce the donor to execute the instrument creating the EPA, or that the attorney is not a suitable person to carry out that role.
If non-compliance issues are identified but not addressed and/or objections are deemed to be well-founded, then the DSS will decline to register the EPA, a decision that may be appealed to the Circuit Court. These measures help to ensure that the attorney is suited to the role and will act in line with the person’s will and preferences.

reply:

Personalised budgets enable individuals to organise and manage their own support arrangements in a manner that best reflects their needs, preferences and goals.

In 2023, responsibility for specialist disability services transferred from the Department of Health to the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth (now the Department of Children, Disability and Equality), and with it, responsibility for the Personalised Budget Demonstrator Pilot.
The Pilot concluded in May 2025 and subsequently entered its evaluation phase, led by the National Disability Authority (NDA). The NDA has produced an evaluation report that is now nearing finalisation. The report sets out key findings from the Pilot, drawing on the experiences of participants, families and other stakeholders.

question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will review HSE guidance and training for adult disability services on the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, particularly how staff should assess and manage foreseeable safety risks when a person wishes to leave a service unaccompanied; how families’ views should be considered, consistent with the person’s rights; and whether she will issue clarification to providers.
reply:
The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act (2015 Act), which commenced in 2023, marked a landmark reform of Ireland’s capacity laws, bringing the state into much closer alignment with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD). The commencement of the 2015 Act represented an important shift away from a ‘best interests’ approach to a rights-based approach, privileging a person’s will, preferences and autonomy.
The 2015 Act brought an end to wardship in the State for adults by repealing the outdated Lunacy Regulation (Ireland) Act 1871 and replacing it with a rights-based model of tiered decision support arrangements. This new suite of tiered decision support arrangements is designed to enable those with diminished decision-making capacity to retain as much control over their own lives as possible, and over the decisions that affect them.
The HSE has developed a range of training and resources for staff across the HSE and HSE-funded services, including disability services, to support the implementation of the 2015 Act in practice. This includes e-learning programmes on supporting decision-making in health and social care, as well as guidance for healthcare workers on applying the legislation in practice.

question: Deputy Cian O'Callaghan asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question 62049/26, if the statutory public consultation process has concluded; if the amendments to the CIÉ pension schemes have been agreed; and when retirees of CIÉ will finally receive their long awaited pension increase.
reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for policy and overall funding in relation to public transport. As a commercial semi-state body, Córas Iompair Éireann (CIÉ) are responsible for the provision of pension schemes for their employees.
Following on from the constructive and collaborative approach of the Trade Union Group and CIÉ management in reaching agreement on a pathway forward as of May 2025, my Department is progressing the agreement of bringing CIÉ pensions onto a more stable footing for the benefit of active, and retired scheme members, including review of the relevant draft Statutory Instruments, and the matter of increases to pension payments.
Under the Transport Act, 1950, a Statutory Consultation process is required regarding amendments to CIÉ Pension Schemes, which took place over the early summer 2026, and representations from interested parties are currently under review.
Every effort is being made to progress this matter at the earliest, keeping in line with the appropriate procedures, compliance with all applicable requirements, and necessary approvals as part of the formal process, which is now well underway and imminent.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the circumstances in which sustainability funding may be provided to an early learning and childcare service required to relocate as a consequence of defective concrete; the categories of expenditure which may be supported under such funding; and whether the funding can contribute towards temporary relocation, long-term relocation or replacement accommodation.
reply:
The sustainability fund for service providers is a support mechanism introduced to ensure the stability and viability of early learning and childcare services for those participating in the Core Funding model. The fund is accessed through a collaborative process involving the service, their local City/County Childcare Committee (CCC), and Pobal, who assess financial eligibility and need.
A childcare service required to relocate due to defective concrete may be eligible for Sustainability Funding under the Emergency Relocation Supports strand. This strand provides community not-for-profit services facing financial difficulty with once-off funding to assist with rental and relocation costs while alternative long-term accommodation is secured.
Once a service engages with their local City/County Childcare Committee, they will be able to avail of supports through the case management process.
Contact details for all City and County Childcare Committees are available on the gov.ie website.

question: Deputy Charles Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the policy measures in place to ensure that childcare capacity is maintained within communities where an existing early learning and childcare facility is affected by defective concrete; and the supports available to prevent the permanent loss of childcare places in such areas.
reply:
The defective concrete blocks issue is an ongoing wider government issue. Responsibility for defective concrete blocks remediation and capital reconstruction rests primarily with other government Departments and local authorities. The Department of Children, Disability and Equality does not have direct responsibility for structural remediation or compensation for defective concrete affected buildings.
However, the Department of Children, Disability and Equality works with Pobal and local Childcare Committees to offer Case Management Supports to services in difficulty. Through this, services may also access Sustainability Funding following an assessment of need. question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the additional measures that can be introduced to prevent the illegal hunting of livestock by lurcher hounds in the Loop Head peninsula.

Legislative and policy responsibility for the Control of Dogs Acts transferred to my Department on 01 June 2025 and for the Dog Breeding Establishments Act on 01 August 2025. This fulfilled a Programme for Government commitment to centralise all legislation and policy in relation to the control of dogs, dog welfare and dog breeding establishments rests with my Department.

This funding will not necessarily cover the full cost of hiring additional dog wardens but is meant as a contribution towards same. question: Deputy Pádraig Mac Lochlainn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine if he will designate Greencastle Harbour, County Donegal as a pelagic landing port for catches over ten tonnes, considering the safety concerns for those vessels that currently have to land at the next nearest designated harbour in Killybegs.
reply:
I am advised that a key component of Ireland's Control Plan, operated by the Sea Fisheries Protection Authority (SFPA), currently in force for pelagic landings is that of pre-transport, control-supervised weighing undertaken on publicly-owned weighbridges - which Greencastle port does not have at present.
In light of this, there are no current plans to designate Greencastle port in the manner suggested by the Deputy.
However, I would also like to assure the Deputy that the designation of ports for landings does not preclude vessels from coming into ports for force majeure reasons such as safe harbour.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine to list the number of engagements between his Department and the European Commission in relation to the next forestry programme.
reply:
The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) contains a general prohibition on the use of State aid to prevent distorting the internal market. This requires submission of a formal application under the Guidelines for State aid in the agricultural and forestry sectors and in rural areas. All efforts are directed towards building on the potential contained in our current Forestry Programme 2023-2027 for the post 2027 period, so that we can continue to deliver lasting benefits for climate change, biodiversity, wood production, economic development alongside quality of life.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine given the importance of afforestation towards climate change mitigation, if his Department will conduct annual reviews when targets are constantly missed in order to address shortcomings, if changes are advised.
reply:
The 2024 Climate Action Plan recognises that afforestation is one of the largest land-based, long-term climate change mitigation measures available to Ireland and sets out the Government’s target of 8,000 hectares of new forestry per year.
The Forestry Programme 2023–2027 provides the implementation mechanism through financial incentives and a range of different forest types available to landowners for afforestation. The 8,000 hectare target is an ambitious one, as forestry remains demand led and is a complex land use choice which is not solely based on incentives. Progress towards this target is closely monitored and my Department are continually developing opportunities to increase the rate of planting.
Last year, my Department prepared a Forestry Opportunities Map which incorporates environmental considerations and associated mapping layers relevant to the Forestry Programme 2023–2027. The Forestry Opportunities Map fed into the Land Use Review (Phase 1 and 2) which forms part of the Programme for Government. The map identifies areas most suitable for planting, primarily based on environmental considerations and soil productivity.
Further, in March this year my Department published the results of a Mid-Term Review of the Forestry Programme 2023–2027. This included a comprehensive package of financial and administrative measures which provided for increases in grants and premia in key areas including forest roads, fencing and agroforestry. question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine in the context of negotiations on revising the EU Animal Transport Regulation, increasingly frequent extreme heat events, the position Ireland is taking on proposed temperature requirements; and if Ireland supports species/category-specific temperature ranges based on EFSA evidence (details supplied).
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 484, 486 and 488 together.
In December 2023, the EU Commission published a legislative proposal for new rules on the protection of animals during transport, to replace the current EU Regulation (EC) No 1 of 2005 protection of animals during transport and related matters in the context of the EU’s Farm to Fork Strategy. Ireland is strongly committed to improving animal welfare standards during transport and supports the revision of the EU Regulation for this sector.
Ireland is currently chairing the EU Council Working Party on this proposal as part of its Presidency of the EU Council from 1 July to 31 December 2026. In this context Ireland is committed to act as the honest broker during its tenure and will work on behalf all Member States to reach a consensus on this proposal.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the projected allocation to Ireland under the Common Agricultural Policy in the European Commission's proposal for the Multiannual Financial Framework 2028 to 2034, compared with the allocation for 2021 to 2027, in tabular form; if CAP funding will remain ring fenced under the proposed single national and regional partnership plans.
reply:
In July 2025, the European Commission published its proposals for the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) as part of its wider proposals for the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for the period 2028–2034. These proposals represent a significant structural change to the current model of CAP delivery, as it is proposed that the CAP will form part of a broader National and Regional Partnership Plan (NRPP), which consolidates several EU funding streams under a single framework.
It is important to note that the funding for the CAP forms part of the broader EU budget negotiations, which is negotiated by Finance Ministers, and is ultimately agreed by Heads of State and Government.
Under the proposals, Ireland’s indicative ring-fenced CAP allocation is €8.162 billion, within a total NRPP allocation of €11.4 billion.
Over the current programming period of the Multiannual Financial Framework (2021-2027), Ireland receives approximately €10.7 billion in EU funding for the CAP.
Comparing the proposed allocation for Ireland’s CAP for the 2028-2034 period with the current CAP period is not a like-for-like comparison. Different interventions or schemes are included in the €8.162 billion ringfenced amount, compared to the €10.7 billion figure for 2021-2027.
In addition, the proposed framework is intended to allow Member States the possibility to supplement CAP interventions from the wider NRPP allocation, thereby offering flexibility to address national priorities.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 477, 478, 479, 480 and 482 together.
My Department demands the highest standards of animal welfare at every stage of the animal’s life, including during transport. My Department has continuously reinforced its practical, administrative and legislative measures to protect the welfare of animals during transport, often going beyond the minimum requirements of EU law, for example in terms of extra space for calves, more frequent driver retraining and temperature control.

reply:

The UK remains by far the most important market for Irish agri-food exports, and we also have significant imports from the UK. question: Deputy Martin Kenny asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the number of the 40 new dog warden roles promised that have now been allocated; and if a breakdown of such allocations will be given by Council areas.
reply:

The funding was intended as a contributory allocation towards the hiring of additional dog wardens. The funding was not intended to provide for the full cost of employment, rather to act to defray the overall cost of same. This funding recognises the increased demands in the area of dog control. question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if the National Standards on Accommodation offered to people in the International Protection process apply to all accommodation centres for international protection applicants, including those living in so called "emergency centres" and designated border facilities as proposed under the newly adopted International Protection Act 2026.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 468, 469, 470 and 474 together.
All IPAS accommodation centres are inspected each year, either by HIQA, by Department officials, or by external inspectors commissioned by the Department. The inspection regime, along with a range of other key quality and compliance actions, has been stepped up significantly over the last 18-24 months, as the Department works to improve standards and value for money across the IPAS system. In 2026 to date, 332 inspections have been completed, covering 261 separate properties. These inspections are fully transparent and available online on gov.ie.
The European Communities (Reception Conditions) (Amendment) Regulations 2023 commenced on 9 January 2024 and provide for the Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) to conduct inspections of certain accommodation centres contracted by the Department.
The purpose of HIQA inspections is to ensure that IPAS accommodation centres within its remit are operating in compliance with the National Standards for accommodation offered to people in the international protection process, which were adopted in 2019 and have been in effect since the beginning of 2021.
A centre may no longer fall under HIQA’s remit for inspections following a change in contract. There are currently 34 accommodation centres within HIQA’s inspection remit which may be inspected by HIQA against the National Standards. question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of criminal legal aid certificates granted since 01 July 2026 without an application by a defence solicitor.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 464 and 473 together.
Under the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962, it is the courts, through the judiciary, that are responsible for the granting of legal aid. My Department processes claims for payment received from solicitors under the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme. Accordingly, my department does not hold the specific information sought by the Deputy in relation to legal aid certificates granted and solicitors who did not submit any claims for payment in 2025. However, I can confirm that 764 solicitors received payments in 2025.
My Department significantly simplified the procedures for Criminal Legal Aid panel membership both for solicitors and counsel last year by waiving the requirement to apply yearly to be retained on panels, with the commencement on 26 November 2025 of S.I. 539 of 2025. Solicitors may apply to be placed on the Criminal Legal Aid panel for any county using a single application form, which is processed by a centralised courts office in Castlebar, Co. Mayo. This system, introduced in 2021, replaced the previous requirement to apply separately to individual local court offices.
Since the commencement of the new system, I am informed by the Courts Service that as of 2 October 2026, almost 2,400 new certificates (invoices for payment) for legal aid have issued with an approximate total value of €1.25 million in the District Court.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if Garda vetting is required for staff working in designated accommodation centres for beneficiaries of temporary protection; the complaints process in place in these centres; and the safeguarding measures in place in these centres.
reply:
Garda vetting of employees is a matter for employers to manage in Designated Accommodation Centres, as my Department does not directly employ staff working in accommodation settings for Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection from Ukraine.
It is necessary for accommodation providers who are providing accommodation under contract to my Department to inform themselves of their legal obligations in this regard, and take appropriate steps. Each contractor is responsible for their Child Safeguarding policy and for assessing whether they have an obligation under the National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Act 2012 to vet their staff.
My Department makes specific reference to legal, industry requirements and best practices in contracts agreed with providers, and it is incumbent on providers to adhere to them.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of a family reunification application in respect of a person (details supplied); the reason for the delay in reaching a decision given the length of time since the application was submitted; if the application can be urgently reviewed in light of the serious protection concerns affecting the applicant’s children currently in Pakistan and the reported risk of forced return to Afghanistan; and when a decision is expected.
reply:
The International Protection Family Reunification application for the person referred to by the Deputy has been received by my Department and continues to be processed at this time. All applications are processed in chronological order.
I understand the wait times can be frustrating for applicants, however, I want to assure anyone who has an application submitted that my Department is doing everything possible to progress applications as quickly as possible.
The speed in which a decision can be made largely depends on the quality of the application received. My Department will continue to engage with the applicant for any further information that may be required to assist with the processing of the application.
As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireachtasmail@justice.ie, which has been specifically established for this purpose. This service enables up to date information on such cases to be obtained without the need to seek information by way of the Parliamentary Question process.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration can he provide an update on the drafting of National Cyber Security Bill; and when is it expected this Bill will be published.
reply:
The National Cyber Security Bill transposes the Network and Information Systems Directive (NIS2) into Irish law and will place the National Cyber Security Centre on a statutory footing. NIS2 significantly enhances the cyber security supervision and enforcement regime that is already in place in the State.
In anticipation of having the legislation in place and to ensure that Ireland is ready to fully implement the directive, we have taken significant steps to ensure that various implementing measures are in place. This includes a robust approach to sectoral regulation for the Directive with the designation of National Competent Authorities to carry out enforcement and supervision. National Competent Authorities are already undertaking significant preparations to take on these new functions.
The enactment of the National Cyber Security Bill is a priority for myself and the Government. Officials in my Department continue to work with the Office of Parliamentary Council on the drafting of the Bill, which is at a very advanced stage. I expect to be in a position to bring a Memo to Government shortly seeking approval to publish the Bill and to notify transposition of the NIS2 Directive by the end of 2026.

reply:

The proposed offences will criminalise extreme or violent pornographic material, including depictions of rape or violence causing serious harm to a person and depictions of bestiality or necrophilia. The timeline will depend on completion of drafting, the publication of the Bill and its subsequent passage through the Oireachtas.

reply:
The regulation of the small public service vehicle (SPSV), including the dispatch operator review and maximum fare reviews, is the responsibility of the independent transport regulator, the National Transport Authority (NTA), under the provisions of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 and 2016. I have no role in the day-to-day operations of the SPSV sector.
From a legislative perspective, Section 24 of the Consolidated Taxi Regulation Acts 2013 & 2016 empowers the NTA Board to make a “Maximum Fares Order” fixing the maximum fare that may be charged by the driver of a taxi for any journey. The current maximum fares order took effect in December 2024, and a maximum fare review is carried out approximately every two years. Hackneys and limousines agree their fares in advance and do not use a meter. As set out in the legislation, charging more than this maximum fare can lead to a prosecution, however, charging below the maximum fare is permitted.
I wrote to the NTA in November 2025 to request clarification on the regulatory position on the Uber fixed price fare for the information of taxi operators and public representatives alike. In their response to my letter, the NTA advised me that the charging of a fixed fare is in accordance with the applicable regulations and that they continue to keep the regulatory model under review.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the timeline for introducing revised qualifying and eligibility criteria for individuals seeking access to both civil and criminal legal aid schemes; if his Department plans to amend the financial means-assessment thresholds to ensure greater access to justice; and the current progress of any draft regulations or legislation regarding these changes.
reply:
It is important to distinguish between the Civil Legal Aid Scheme, which is administered by the Legal Aid Board and provides legal aid and advice in civil matters subject to statutory eligibility criteria, and the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme, under which legal aid is granted by the courts through the judiciary in accordance with the Criminal Justice (Legal Aid) Act 1962.
The Legal Aid Board is the statutory, independent body responsible for the provision of civil legal aid and advice to qualifying individuals. The Civil Legal Aid Scheme has two parts: a legal advice element and a legal representation element. Eligibility for the scheme is determined by reference to a financial assessment and the merits of the case being taken. In accordance with the provisions of the Civil Legal Aid Act 1995 (as amended) and associated Regulations, the Legal Aid Board calculates financial eligibility with reference to the applicant’s disposable income and disposable assets after certain allowances are applied to both.
In June 2022, a Civil Legal Aid Review Group under the chairmanship of former Chief Justice Frank Clarke, SC, was established to review the current operation of the Civil Legal Aid Scheme. The outputs of the review were published in July 2025 and contained recommendations relating to eligibility for the Scheme including income threshold and allowances, as well as recommendations aimed at improving access to justice for people.

reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 441 and 443 together.
The Pact provides for a fair, sustainable, and efficient asylum procedure. This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.
The Asylum Border Procedure has a 12-week time limit for first instance and appeal decisions to be completed for applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, or for those who have no documents, false documents, or are deemed a security risk.
Those seeking to claim asylum attend a designated Screening Centre, where they lodge an application for international protection. During the screening process, applicants undergo further security, identity, health and vulnerability checks.
The Screening Centre has staff from asylum processing, appeals, returns, reception, the HSE, the Department of Social Protection, legal representatives and other agencies co-located on site to engage with applicants.
Under the IP Act 2026 consideration of certain categories of applicants must form part of the assessment. These categories include, amongst others, minors, persons with disabilities and pregnant women.

This will be achieved through greater convergence in asylum practices across the EU, including standardised processing times for decisions: six months for a standard procedure, three months for accelerated and border procedures, and two months for inadmissible cases.
The Asylum Border Procedure has a 12-week time limit for first instance and appeal decisions to be completed for applicants from countries of origin with a recognition rate of 20% or less across the EU, or for those who have no documents, false documents, or are deemed a security risk.
Those seeking to claim asylum attend a designated Screening Centre, where they lodge an application for international protection. During the screening process, applicants undergo further security, identity, health and vulnerability checks.
The Screening Centre has staff from asylum processing, appeals, returns, reception, the HSE, the Department of Social Protection, legal representatives and other agencies co-located on site to engage with applicants.
Under the IP Act 2026 consideration of certain categories of applicants must form part of the assessment. These categories include, amongst others, minors, persons with disabilities and pregnant women.

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number applicants under the AMMR strand of the International Protection Act 2026; the number of appeals under AMMR; the outcomes of those appeals; the number transferred to another member State under AMMR.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
The EU Migration and Asylum Pact has been designed to establish a common approach to migration and asylum that is based on the concepts of solidarity and responsibility amongst Member States.
The Asylum and Migration Management Regulation (AMMR) replaces the current “Dublin III Regulation” and improves the system for determining the Member State responsible for asylum applications by making it more efficient and stable, and preventing secondary movements. Key changes include:?
• Shorter deadlines for all procedures, thus contributing to a faster and more efficient process for determining the Member State responsible.
• Introducing the obligation to apply for protection in the Member State of first entry and remain there until the Member State responsible is determined. Lack of compliance with this obligation will lead to important consequences, like providing only for basic needs rather than the full reception conditions.
• Making the ‘take-back’ procedure for returning someone from one Member State to another more effective, in particular by introducing shorter time limits and no shift of responsibility in case the take-back notification is not sent on time.
• Reinforcing family criteria, among others by:
• Including families formed in transit before they arrive in the EU;
• Introducing the possibility to establish responsi

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the legal basis for the issuing of a labour market access permit to an international protection applicant under the international protection act 2026.
reply:
Prior to 12th June 2026, Article 15 of the 2013 Reception Conditions Directive (Directive 2013/33/EU) formed the legal basis on which applicants for international protection were granted labour market access.
Article 15 of the 2013 Directive was transposed into Irish law by the European Communities (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2018 (S.I. No. 230 of 2018) as amended by S.I. No. 436 of 2020, S.I. No. 52 of 2021, S.I. No. 178 of 2021, S.I. No. 31 of 2022, and S.I. No. 649 of 2023.
Under S.I. No. 230 of 2018 as amended, people are eligible to apply for labour market access permission if:
• They are an international protection applicant under the 2015 Act; and
• They have waited at least 5 months from their “Application Received” date for their first instance recommendation; and
• They are cooperating with the international protection process – delays in receiving a first instance recommendation within 6 months must not be attributed, or attributed in part, to the applicant
• They have not received a final decision on their application.
Following that, a person may be issued a permission for labour market access if, at 6 months, they have not yet received a first instance recommendation. This permission is valid for 12 months and may be renewed until a final decision is made on the person's international protection application.
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 came into effect on 12 June 2026 and gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum P

question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of implicit withdrawals under the International Protection Act 2026; the reason for the decisions; the number of appeals; the outcomes of those appeals.
reply:
As the Deputy will be aware, the International Protection Act 2026 gives effect to the EU Migration and Asylum Pact and came into effect on 12 June 2026.
An application for international protection may be deemed to have been implicitly withdrawn for a number of reasons relating to an applicant's failure to qualify for, comply with, or engage with the international protection process. The grounds on which an application may be considered implicitly withdrawn are set out in section 71 of the International Protection Act 2026 and include, among other matters, a failure to lodge an application, failure to attend a scheduled interview, failure to comply with reporting requirements, or failure to remain available to the competent authorities.
Since the commencement of the Act until , 179 implicit withdrawal decisions have been made by the International Protection Office.
The grounds on which those decisions were made are as follows:
• 143 decisions under section 71(1)(a);
• 30 decisions under section 71(1)(d); and
• 6 decisions under section 71(1)(f).
Of the 179 decisions made, two have been appealed to the Tribunal of Asylum and Return Appeals (TARA). Both appeals remain active.

question: Deputy Pat the Cope Gallagher asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration when the District and Circuit Court will return to Donegal town courthouse.
reply:
Management of the courts and operational matters, including matters pertaining to the maintenance and use of court buildings, are the responsibility of the Courts Service, which is independent in the exercise of theses functions.
I am advised by the Courts Service that Donegal Courthouse was temporarily closed in September 2025 following significant health and safety concerns identified by the Office of Public Works (OPW). The most serious issues relate to the entrances for both the public and the judiciary, including a partial collapse of the ceiling in the public entrance porch. In the interests of public safety, all sittings scheduled for Donegal are being accommodated at Ballyshannon Courthouse on a temporary basis.
Since then, the Courts Service has been working closely with the OPW to determine the scope of remedial works and associated costs. I am advised that, following a request from the Courts Service, the OPW carried out a full building condition survey of Donegal Courthouse. The report was provided to the Courts Service in January of 2026 for their consideration.
I am further advised that at this stage, the building condition assessment is part of an ongoing process of technical evaluation and options development being undertaken. The findings are being used to inform decision making on potential remediation and investment options, and further information will be made available as the process progresses and key decisions are reached.

question: Deputy Robert O'Donoghue asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the number of complaints or disclosures received by An Garda Síochána to date in 2026 relating to sex-for-rent arrangements following the enactment of the new legislation; the number of cases referred for investigation or prosecution for such incidents; and if he will provide a breakdown by Garda division where available.
reply:
Offering or advertising accommodation in exchange for sexual activity, or “sex for rent”, is a criminal offence. I secured the introduction of this measure through the Criminal Law, Civil Law and Defence (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 in July 2026. Part 15 of the Act, which addresses the issue of “sex for rent”, was commenced on 1 September 2026.
The Act introduces two specific criminal offences around ‘sex for rent’ – offering accommodation in exchange for sexual activity and the advertising of accommodation in exchange for sexual activity. The provisions encompass both rental agreements between landlords and tenants, and ‘rent-a-room’ situations. It is the offer or advertisement that is being criminalised - there is no requirement to prove that sexual activity occurred. The proposed penalty for these offences is a Class A fine of up to €5,000.
The legislation delivers on a specific Programme for Government commitment and forms part of broader efforts to address domestic, sexual and gender-based violence and abuse.
I have been advised by An Garda Síochána that work is currently underway to provide a structured mechanism which will allow for the recording of complaints, disclosures and incidents relating to sex-for-rent arrangements.

question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Social Protection if it is possible to introduce a reduced rate of employers' PRSI for employees under the age of 24, to incentivise the employment of young people.
reply:
In general, the issue of targeted supports to incentivise the employment of young people is a matter for the Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment. However, the following is the position with regards to employer PRSI.
The main finding of the latest Actuarial Review of the Social Insurance Fund was that the Fund will experience significant long term sustainability challenges. It is in this regard that the previous Government agreed to a series of annual incremental increases in all PRSI rates, including employer PRSI, up to and including 2028. A further evaluation of the position of the Fund will be held after the completion of the next Actuarial Review next year.
It is in this context that there are no proposals, nor has consideration has been given to reduce the employer PRSI rate for employees of any age group. However, in recognition of the pressures faced by businesses, the Government agreed, in Budget 2026, to increase the employer PRSI threshold from €527 to €552 per week, effective from 1 January 2026. This will ensure that employers with full time employees on the national minimum wage or employees with earnings under €552 per week will attract the lower employer PRSI rate of 9%.
Any further changes to the PRSI employer rates or threshold would have to be considered in a budgetary context, taking account of the economic circumstances and with a view to the sustainability of the Social Insurance Fund.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection whether consideration has been given to a waste collection support for State pensioners living alone, in view of annual minimum bin charges exceeding one week's pension.
reply:
The matter of waste collection charges is the responsibility of my colleague the Minister for the Environment, Climate and Communications. The waste management market in Ireland is now serviced by private companies, where prices charged are matters between those companies and their customers, subject to compliance with all applicable environmental and other relevant legislation, including contract and consumer legislation.
However, my Department does provide Additional Needs Payments as part of the Supplementary Welfare Allowance scheme for people who have essential expenses, which they cannot meet from their own resources.
The decision process involves consideration of the need presented and the ability of the person and their household to meet that need. This entails an assessment, as opposed to a specific means test, of an applicant’s weekly household income, their savings and investments, their outgoings and the type of assistance needed. Other State supports that may already be available to the person are also considered. This ensures that support is provided to people with the greatest financial need.
Any person who considers that they may have an entitlement to an Additional Needs Payment is encouraged to contact their local community welfare service. There is a National Community Welfare Contact Centre in place - 0818-607080 - which will direct callers to the appropriate office. In addition, applications can be made online via www.mywelfare.ie.

question: Deputy John Connolly asked the Minister for Social Protection when the comprehensive review of means testing within the social protection system commenced; the status of that review; when he expects the review to be completed and its finding published; and the reasons for the length of time taken to complete the review.
reply:
The Programme for Government commits to carry out a comprehensive review of means tests across the social welfare system taking into account the Report on Means Testing by the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Social Protection. My Department is conducting a review of means testing within the social protection system.
The aim is to examine various means-tested schemes and identify any issues related to their respective means tests. With over 140 schemes and services, many of which are means-tested, this is a complex and detailed task.
It is my intention that the review's findings will inform decisions regarding potential changes to means testing in future Budgets.
The review is currently with senior management of the Department for review and I expect that it will be submitted to me shortly.
Due to the complexity of the review, I will carefully and thoroughly evaluate it to determine the best way to utilise its findings and identify those that may warrant further consideration.
However, any prospective changes to means-testing arrangements will need to be evaluated and considered within the overall policy and budgetary context.

The person concerned was notified of this decision in writing on 26 June 2026 and afforded the right of review and/or appeal.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection further to Parliamentary Question No. 6110/26, to provide the actual outstanding social welfare overpayment debt balance owed to his Department at the end of each year from 2016 to 2025, inclusive; and the amount written off in each of those years.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 411 and 412 together.
In 2025, the Department of Social Protection spent €27.4 billion on income supports, employment services and related programmes. During the year, almost 89 million payments were issued and more than 3.7 million applications were processed across the department's core schemes and services.
The overall value of overpayments raised in any given year represent less than 0.5% of total expenditure.
A structured debt management policy in line with normal good practice in recovery of overpayments operates within my Department. Persons who have been overpaid social welfare have a liability to refund the overpayment as they have been in receipt of a payment to which they were not entitled.

In general, overpayments of deceased customers are only written off where there are not sufficient funds in the estate to repay the overpayment.
The Department seeks to recover the full value by deducting instalments from on-going weekly payments or requires a repayment plan to be agreed where a person is no longer receiving a Social Welfare payment. Where a person does not engage with the Department to agree a repayment plan, the Department has powers of attachments to a person’s earnings or to funds held in financial institutions to recover an overpayment.

question: Deputy Peadar Tóibín asked the Minister for Social Protection the proportion of the total social welfare overpayments raised in each of the years 2016 to 2025 that was attributable to proven fraud, customer error and official or administrative error respectively; and the monetary value associated with each category.
reply:
The Department of Social Protection administers approximately 140 schemes and programmes, and while most payments are correct, overpayments can sometimes occur for a variety of reasons.
In general, the majority of overpayments are a result of customer error, where information that affects entitlement to payments is not provided in a timely manner resulting in small overpayments.
Debt holders are made aware that a social welfare debt will remain on their records until fully recovered. This will result in a reduction of all future entitlements up to, and including pension. Following the death of a customer owing a debt, the Department will have a claim on any estate remaining.

Following correspondence received on 23 July 2026, the case was reviewed. As a result of this review, it was established that the person was working fewer than 18.5 hours per week and CA was awarded from 16 July 2026.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection if she will review the treatment of inherited capital in the means test for disability allowance where the recipient has a lifelong disability and the inheritance is intended to fund their long-term care and independent living; the number of recipients whose payment was reduced or ceased due to inherited capital in each of the past three years.
reply:
Disability Allowance is my Department's primary disability related social assistance scheme. It is a means-tested payment for people with a disability who are aged between 16 and 66. In order to be eligible, the disability must have continued for at least one year or be expected to continue for at least one year.
In addition, the person must be substantially restricted from doing work that would otherwise be suitable for a person of their age, experience, and qualifications. Eligibility for the payment is also subject to a habitual residency requirement.
Social welfare legislation provides that, for means-tested social assistance schemes, all income and assets belonging to the claimant, and their spouse or partner, where applicable, is assessable. This recognises the fact that couples operate as a single household and can share living expenses in a manner not available to a single person.
The purpose of a means test is to ensure that scarce resources are directed to those with the greatest need and it supports an economically sustainable and socially equitable allocation of scarce resources
Disability Allowance has one of the highest capital disregards operated by my Department. A recipient can have up to €50,000 in savings and still receive the full rate of payment. This is compared to a €20,000 disregard for most social welfare payments. The person was notified of this decision in writing on 21 July 2026 and was advised of their right to seek a review and/or appeal the decision.
An appeal was subsequently lodged with the independent Social Welfare Appeals Office (SWAO) on 27 August 2026, accompanied by additional medical evidence.

question: Deputy Michael Healy-Rae asked the Minister for Social Protection the steps a school (details supplied) should take, now that they cannot source a provider for hot or cold school meals.
reply:
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week.
All schools as independent contracting authorities are responsible for choosing their school meals supplier on the open market, in a fair and transparent manner in accordance with public procurement rules.
In the case of the school referred to by the Deputy, my Department is aware of the difficulties experienced in securing a provider. Departmental officials have been in contact with the school and have engaged with local meals on wheels to support them source a supplier.
Officials have also explored the possibility of a collaborative procurement arrangement with neighbouring schools and will continue to work with the school to identify any viable options. My Department remains available to support the school in its efforts to secure a provider and will continue to engage with the school and relevant stakeholders on this matter.
I want to assure the Deputy that my Department will continue to work with the school concerned to explore all available options with a view to facilitating participation in the School Meals Programme as soon as possible.

question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Social Protection if he is aware of the difficulties being experienced by families who are being refused fuel allowance on household means grounds where adult children remain living in the family home due to the lack of affordable rental accommodation and housing options; whether consideration is being given to amending the means assessment for fuel allowance in such cases.
reply:
The criteria for Fuel Allowance are framed in order to direct the limited resources available to the department in as targeted a manner as possible. To qualify for the Fuel Allowance payment, a person must satisfy all the qualifying criteria.
Fuel Allowance operates as part of an overall system of social protection supports which provides assistance payments based on a system of means testing. The means test ensures that the recipient has a verifiable income need and that resources are targeted to those who need them most.
For those who apply and are aged 66 or over, only the means of the applicant and, if applicable, their spouse, civil partner or cohabitant is included when assessing means for Fuel Allowance purposes. However, the normal household composition criteria apply.
A change in the qualifying criteria such as including adult children who are in employment and not in receipt of a qualifying social protection payment, would have to be considered in the context of scheme policy and budgetary negotiations. Disregarding a household member who is not reliant on long term social protection payments and who is in employment would change the targeted nature of the scheme.

To address this challenge, I commissioned two independent reviews of the School Meals Programme. The Nutrition Review of the Hot School Meals Scheme, undertaken by a CORU-registered dietitian under the clinical supervision of the Department of Health, and IPSOS Behaviour and Attitudes School Meals Survey 2026, a national survey of pupils, parents, teachers, principals and suppliers.

The Nutrition Review found that food waste remains a challenge, with absenteeism, meal preferences and ordering practices identified as key contributing factors.
The Nutrition Review outlined several key recommendations aimed directly at waste reduction and food management.

question: Deputy Jen Cummins asked the Minister for Social Protection the specific action he is taking to move school meals (details supplied) towards a model where meals are cooked from fresh raw ingredients from scratch in one kitchen, and away from the current predominant ‘assembly and reheat’ model used in the Irish school meal programme.
reply:
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week. 11 Meals on Wheels providers are currently supporting 40 schools in the Hot School Meals scheme.
The vast majority of primary schools in Ireland do not have on site food preparation or catering facilities. The Report on Nutrition Review of the Hot School Meals Scheme, found that only a small proportion of schools audited operated a fresh on-site kitchen model.
The School Meals programme is designed so that meals are provided by contracted food business operators. This ensures responsibility for food safety and legislative compliance is placed on these professional providers and not on the schools themselves. This also ensures children benefit from a reliable, high-quality service, while schools are protected from having to take on responsibilities more appropriate to the providers, who will have the necessary expertise and experience in food provision.
The recently published Report on Nutrition Review of the Hot School Meals Scheme examined the different catering systems in operation. The review found that hot-drop delivery models, particularly where meals are cooked fresh and delivered hot to schools, were associated with higher quality meals and lower levels of waste. question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Social Protection If he will address the concerns raised in correspondence details attached regarding the financial difficulties experienced by households where a person remains unable to return to work following cancer treatment and is approaching the end of their illness benefit entitlement.
reply:
Illness Benefit is the primary short term income support provided by my Department to those who are unable to work due to illness of any type and who are covered by social insurance. Eligibility for Illness Benefit depends on the person’s PRSI record and class. It is available for up to two years for people who have the required social insurance contributions under PRSI class A, E, H or P.
Where a person exhausts their entitlement to payment of Illness Benefit and is expected to remain unfit to attend work for a further period of at least 12 months, they have the option of making an application for Invalidity Pension, which is another social insurance scheme paid from the Social Insurance Fund. Eligibility is based on PRSI contributions and medical condition. To qualify, the person must have been incapable of work for at least 12 months and be likely to be incapable of work for at least another 12 months or they must be permanently incapable of work.
Where a person is in a position to return to work to some degree following a period of at least six months in receipt of Illness Benefit they may be eligible for Partial Capacity Benefit. A person may qualify for Partial Capacity Benefit if their restriction on capacity for work is assessed as moderate, severe, or profound. The rate of payment made is dependent on the level of restriction determined in the medical assessment. Where this is deemed to be mild, the person is not eligible for payment. question: Deputy Mairéad Farrell asked the Minister for Social Protection if his attention has been drawn to pension entitlements for staff in voluntary residential and aftercare services, which have been effectively frozen since the financial collapse; if he is aware of the serious recruitment and retention challenges this has created within the sector which may leave voluntary care services at risk of closure; and if he will consider providing entitlement for voluntary social care staff to the State pension scheme.
reply:
The Department of Social Protection is responsible for the State pension system, which is made up of the social insurance-based State Pension (Contributory) and the means tested State Pension (Non-Contributory).
Employees in voluntary residential and aftercare services are covered by the social insurance system according to the PRSI class applicable to their employment. Employees who pay full-rate PRSI may qualify for the State Pension (Contributory) and other social insurance benefits, subject to the relevant qualifying conditions.
The State Pension (Contributory) is not means tested and may be paid alongside earnings or an occupational pension. Where a person does not qualify for the contributory pension, or qualifies only at a reduced rate, they may apply for the State Pension (Non-Contributory), subject to the relevant means and residency conditions.
State pension entitlement is separate from occupational pension provision. My Department has no role in determining occupational pension arrangements for employees of voluntary organisations or in extending membership of a public service pension scheme to a particular group of voluntary-sector employees.
The recruitment and retention issues raised by the Deputy concern the funding and staffing of voluntary residential and aftercare services. reply:

question: Deputy Pat Buckley asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment for an immediate national moratorium on grid connections for data centres.
reply:
Data centres are fundamental to Ireland’s position as a leading global hub for digital and technology-driven enterprise. They form a critical part of the State’s digital infrastructure, supporting activities including cloud computing, artificial intelligence, financial services and public sector digital services. Their economic footprint is substantial with €104 billion in gross value added (around 20% of Ireland’s economy) enabled by data-centre-dependent sectors, approximately 183,000 people working in Ireland’s ICT sector and around 19,500 jobs directly in data centre construction and operations.
While data centres are large energy users, unlike other European countries that have heavy-industry bases, Ireland’s industrial electricity demand is primarily concentrated in our digital economy. This is our core energy-intensive industry. The Government is committed to delivering a balanced approach to facilitate the sustainable growth of data centres, whilst achieving the twin objective of decarbonisation and digitalisation and ensuring overall energy security and affordability for consumers and businesses.

Where land is leased, the means assessment is based on the persons net income from the lease, calculated by deducting allowable expenses from the gross rental income. Where land is neither farmed nor leased and is not otherwise productively used, it is assessed on its capital value in accordance with the statutory means test provisions applicable to state pension non-contributory.

My Department regularly reviews its schemes and policies to ensure that they continue to provide effective support and respond to changing demographic, social and economic conditions.

question: Deputy Ciarán Ahern asked the Minister for Social Protection the reason founders of social enterprises established as companies limited by guarantee may be classified as self-employed and required to pay Class S PRSI, despite being paid through payroll, holding no shares in the organisation and being accountable to a voluntary board of directors; if this classification excludes them from MyFutureFund; the steps available to correct an inappropriate classification; and if he will review the rules in order that social enterprise founders are supported to save for retirement rather than penalised for establishing organisations they do not own.
reply: The correct insurability of a person who is a founder of a social enterprise which is established as a company limited by guarantee will depend on the facts and circumstances of the engagement. In general, workers who are engaged on a contract of service (employee) basis and who are the beneficial owner of a company or who are able to control 50 per cent or more of the ordinary share capital of the company which they work for are required to pay class S PRSI in accordance with Paragraph 7 of Part 2 of Schedule 1 of the SWCA 2005. As CLG’s do not have any share capital, Scope Section make decisions on the correct classification of workers engaged by a CLG on a case-by-case basis, in accordance with Social Welfare legislation and the Code of Practice on Determining Employment Status. It is open to any individual seeking a decision regarding their own insurability to apply to Scope Section for a formal decision at any time.

question: Deputy Catherine Callaghan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he is satisfied that communities affected by strategic infrastructure developments, SIDs, have adequate opportunities to participate in the planning process; and if he will outline any proposals to enhance public participation.
reply:
Section 37E of the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended (Act of 2000) sets out the public participation procedure in relation to Strategic Infrastructure Development (SID). Specifically section 37E(3)(a)(ii) of the Act of 2000 requires newspaper notices for SID specifying the times and places at which, and the period (not being less than 6 weeks) during which, a copy of the application and the environmental impact assessment report may be inspected free of charge or purchased on payment of a specified fee (which fee shall not exceed the reasonable cost of making such copy), section 37E(3)(a)(iii) of the Act of 2000 invites the making, during such period, of submissions and observations by the public to An Coimisiún Pleanála (the Commission).
Additionally, section 134 of the Act of 2000 provides the Commission may in its absolute discretion, hold an oral hearing of an application for SID under section 37E of the Act of 2000. These provisions ensure public participation in applications for SID and these will be maintained when the Planning and Development Act 2024 is commenced.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will ask Met Éireann to examine whether the existing weather monitoring network adequately captures localised wind speeds and severe weather conditions in the Laune Valley and Killorglin area, particularly given the surrounding mountainous topography.
reply:
Met Éireann’s key mission is to monitor, analyse and predict Ireland's weather, flooding, and climate, and to provide Irish society and decisionmakers with information to protect life and property.
In keeping with this mission, Met Éireann carries out forecast verification to evaluate the performance of its forecasts compared to the actual observed conditions. This is carried out across Met Éireann’s entire forecast area on an ongoing basis. Findings from these evaluations are used in the refinement of Met Éireann’s weather models and to help inform the development of its observation networks countrywide.

question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage when Ireland’s draft nature restoration plan submitted to the European Commission on 1 September 2026 will be made publicly available.
reply:
The EU Nature Restoration Law (NRL) entered into force on 18 August 2024. It sets out a framework for EU Member States to restore nature, with binding targets for the restoration of a wide range of ecosystems including rivers, forests, oceans, urban and agricultural areas, as well as protected habitats and species. Ireland had until 1 September 2026 to submit a draft National Restoration Plan to the EU Commission, setting out how we intend to achieve these legally binding targets.
The draft National Restoration Plan (NRP) template was submitted to the European Commission on the 1 September 2026. The draft NRP template is very technical. An accessible version of the draft NRP submitted to the European Commission along with a detailed guide is currently being drafted and will be made publicly available once complete.
In early 2027 the EU Commission will submit formal feedback on the NRP, and the draft NRP will be revised based on this feedback. In September 2027, the final National Restoration Plan template will be submitted to the EU Commission.

reply:

Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended.
The 2011 Regulations prescribe maximum net income limits for each local authority, in different bands according to the area concerned, with income being defined and assessed according to a standard Household Means Policy.
The Policy provides for a range of income disregards and local authorities also have discretion to disregard income that is once-off, temporary or short-term in nature and which is outside the regular pattern of a person’s annual income. The income bands are expressed in terms of a maximum net income threshold for a single-person household, with an allowance of 5% for each additional adult household member, subject to a maximum allowance under this category of 10% and separately a 2.5% allowance for each child.
The baseline social housing income thresholds are €40,000, €35,000 and €30,000 for Bands 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Cork County is in Band 2 which is €35,000. These thresholds are net income i.e. gross household income less income tax, PRSI, Universal Social Charge and Additional Superannuation Contribution.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if consideration will be given to installing an automatic weather station or other appropriate monitoring equipment in the lower foothills of the MacGillycuddy’s Reeks, County Kerry to improve monitoring of local wind conditions in the Laune Valley and Killorglin area.
reply:
Met Éireann’s key mission is to monitor, analyse and predict Ireland's weather, flooding, and climate, and to provide Irish society and decisionmakers with information to protect life and property.
Met Éireann’s observation networks are a vital component in the delivery of this mission. Met Éireann manages a broad range of observation networks including weather stations, climate stations, rainfall stations, weather radars and environmental samplers. The location and density of these networks is governed by a range of complex factors including forecast and operational impact, climate requirements, site suitability and representativeness, amongst a range of others. Met Éireann is continuously developing and enhancing its observation networks countrywide. Careful consideration is and will be given to locations where additional monitoring will be beneficial to Met Éireann’s mission.

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if there are plans for lands (details supplied) purchased by the Land Development Agency; when is it planned these lands will be developed and approximately; and the number of homes planned for these lands.
reply:
The Land Development Agency (LDA) plays a key role in the delivery of new housing under the Government’s Housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities.
The Agency is actively developing housing on State lands and market acquired lands and working in partnership with local authorities to develop large scale mixed tenure schemes of starter homes for purchase and rent, along with social housing on local authority owned sites.
The 86-hectare site at Lissenhall, Swords, Co. Dublin was acquired by the LDA from the National Asset Management Agency (NAMA) in October 2025. The land, which includes the proposed MetroLink Estuary terminus, has the potential to deliver c.6,000 homes, alongside new commercial and community amenities.
The LDA is a statutory body under the aegis of my Department and in line with section 12(4) of the Act is independent in the performance of its functions.
It may be helpful to note that arrangements have been put in place by my Department to ensure that public bodies under its aegis have a dedicated email address in place to facilitate the provision of information directly to members of the Oireachtas. This provides a speedy, efficient and cost effective system to address queries directly to the relevant bodies. In this regard, the LDA can be contacted by emailing oireachtas@lda.ie.

reply:
A key priority under the Governments Starter Homes Programme is the scaling up of the delivery of affordable Starter Homes for purchase, aimed at first time buyers and some fresh start applicants, through the local authorities and the Land Development Agency. Section 487 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 provides that a person who organises a funfair or owns fairground equipment shall not make available for public use any fairground equipment unless a valid certificate of safety has been granted in respect of that equipment. question: Deputy Naoise Ó Muirí asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if he will consider, as part of Budget 2027, increasing the funding available under the vacant property refurbishment grant and derelict property top-up grant; if an increase is being actively examined in light of rising construction and refurbishment costs.
reply:
Addressing vacancy and dereliction is a key priority for this Government, as reflected in the Housing Plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities. The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, funded under the Croí Cónaithe Towns Fund, has been a key measure in addressing vacancy and dereliction across the country.
The Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant provides a grant of up to €50,000 to support the refurbishment of vacant properties for occupation as a principal private residence and for properties which will be made available for rent. A top-up grant of up to €20,000 is available where the property is confirmed to be derelict, bringing the total grant available for a derelict property up to a maximum of €70,000. In order to qualify for the grant, the property must be vacant for two years or more at the time of application.
To the end of Q2 2026, over 18,800 applications have been received, over 14,300 approved, with more than 6,300 grants paid out following completion of works, totalling almost €349 million.
The maximum grant amounts were increased in May 2023 from €30,000 to €50,000 for the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant and from €50,000 to €70,000 for homes considered derelict.
In conjunction with the Vacant Property Refurbishment Grant, other supports and grants may be used supporting bringing these vacant and derelict properties into use as homes.

question: Deputy James O'Connor asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if his Department will consider increasing the current income limit thresholds for eligibility for social housing for Cork County.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 363 and 376 together.
Applications for social housing support are assessed by the relevant local authority, in accordance with the eligibility and need criteria set down in section 20 of the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2009 and the associated Social Housing Assessment Regulations 2011, as amended.
The 2011 Regulations prescribe maximum net income limits for each local authority, in different bands according to the area concerned, with income being defined and assessed according to a standard Household Means Policy.
The Policy provides for a range of income disregards and local authorities also have discretion to disregard income that is once-off, temporary or short-term in nature and which is outside the regular pattern of a person’s annual income. The income bands are expressed in terms of a maximum net income threshold for a single-person household, with an allowance of 5% for each additional adult household member, subject to a maximum allowance under this category of 10% and separately a 2.5% allowance for each child.
The baseline social housing income thresholds are €40,000, €35,000 and €30,000 for Bands 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Cork County is in Band 2 which is €35,000. These thresholds are net income i.e. gross household income less income tax, PRSI, Universal Social Charge and Additional Superannuation Contribution.
My Department has been examining the existing income limits in the context of current market and household inc
