question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her response to the recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 47 and 90 together.
The Government has strongly condemned Russia’s attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August.
This activity is part of a clear trend. It forms part of a broader, coordinated, and long-standing hybrid campaign aimed at threatening and undermining the security, resilience and democratic foundations of the EU, its Member States and its partners.
In response to the Leipzig incident, I expressed my full solidarity with Germany, and with all Member States affected by Russia’s reckless and increasingly frequent hybrid attacks. I discussed the issue with the HRVP, Kaja Kallas, and my German and other EU counterparts at the meeting of EU Foreign Ministers I hosted in Druid's Glen in early September.
The Ambassador of the Russian Federation was summoned by senior officials of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade on 3 September to hear expression of Ireland’s strong condemnation. Many of our EU partners also did so. Russia’s attempts to divide us and to weaken our support for Ukraine will not succeed.
Ireland is extremely concerned at the continued increased in hybrid activity. Russia’s actions threaten the security of EU citizens, as well as regional stability and international peace.
We support the full use of all tools available to prevent, deter, and respond to Russia’s hybrid activities, including through sanctions.

question: Deputy Cormac Devlin asked the Minister for Health whether she will extend publicly funded pneumococcal vaccination to carers, frontline health and social care workers and all adults aged 50 years and over; and whether the National Immunisation Advisory Committee has been asked to advise on replacing the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine with a conjugate vaccine, such as PCV20, for adults, as has happened in the UK programme.
reply:
The National Immunisation Programme in Ireland is based on the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). The committee's recommendations are based on the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland and international best practice in relation to immunisation. NIAC make recommendations on vaccination policy to the Department of Health.
The National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC) currently recommends pneumococcal vaccination for adults aged 65 years and older and for adults aged 18-64 years with risk factors for invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD). These risk factors are outlined in Chapter 16 (Pneumococcal infection) of the Immunisation Guidelines for Ireland (Table 16.1) and include populations living with certain chronic diseases, immunocompromise and social and occupational risk factors. NIAC currently does not routinely recommend pneumococcal vaccination for healthcare workers or for adults aged 50-64 years in the general population.
The type of pneumococcal vaccine recommended depends on age and underlying risk factors. Older adults aged 65 years and above without additional risk factors for IPD are currently recommended to receive the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23). Some adult populations who NIAC categorise to be at high-risk of IPD are recommended to receive both PPV23 and a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13).

question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Health if she will consider increasing the means threshold for over 70s medical cards due to cost-of-living pressures.
reply:
Medical card provision is primarily based on financial assessment. In accordance with the Health Act 1970 (as amended), eligibility for a medical card is determined by the HSE, which assesses each application on a qualifying financial threshold. This is the amount of money that an individual can earn per week and still qualify for a card. It is specific to the individual’s own financial circumstances.
People under 70 are assessed under the general means tested medical card thresholds which are based on an applicant’s household income after deduction of tax, PRSI and Universal Social Charge. Certain expenses are also taken into account. Detailed guidelines are available at: [Assessment for a medical card] (www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/applying/assessment/)People aged 70 or older are assessed under medical card income thresholds which are based on gross income. However, those aged over 70 can also be assessed under the general means tested scheme where there are particularly high medical costs. Details are available at: Medical card for over 70s (www2.hse.ie/services/schemes-allowances/medical-cards/other-types-of-medical-card/over-70s/).
Every effort is made by the HSE, within the framework of the legislation, to support applicants in applying for a medical card - in particular, to take full account of difficult circumstances in the case of applicants who may be in excess of the income guidelines. question: Deputy Roderic O'Gorman asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade the actions she intends to take to raise the recent crackdown on LGBTQ+ activists in the Republic of Türkiye.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 29, 46 and 75 together.
I am deeply concerned about recent measures, including legal proceedings and arrests, against LGBTIQ+ organisations and persons in Türkiye. As an EU candidate country, member of the Council of Europe, and a party to international human rights instruments, Türkiye is expected to uphold the highest democratic standards and to ensure the respect of fundamental rights for all, including for LGBTIQ+ persons.
Every person, regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity, or any other characteristic, is entitled to equality, dignity and the full enjoyment of their human rights. The promotion and protection of the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is a domestic and foreign policy priority for Ireland, and this is reflected in our campaign for membership of the UN Human Rights Council, where defending the rights of LGBTIQ+ persons is one of our five thematic priorities.
Ireland continues to support initiatives in the EU and other international fora which promote and protect the rights of LGBTIQ+ people, and which condemn violence and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Ireland stands in full solidarity with LGBTIQ+ persons and their allies in Türkiye. As part of ongoing bilateral engagement, Ireland raises human rights issues, including regarding LGBTIQ+ persons, with the Turkish authorities.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Health the current full year overspend forecast for the HSE in 2026 held by her Department; whether a supplementary estimate will be sought and the amount; the specific expenditure controls introduced since June 2026; and the savings each has delivered to date.
reply:
At the end of August, the Health Service Executive (HSE) reported a cash deficit of €696 million. Expenditure was 9.0% higher than in the same period last year, compared with an increase of 5.1% in the available budget. This position is not sustainable.
There are genuine pressures on the health service, including increased demand, an ageing population, inflation and rising medicines and treatment costs. However, these factors do not explain the full scale of the overspend.
My Department and the HSE are closely monitoring the financial position. Additional expenditure controls have been in place since April and June, and a stronger and more targeted control response is now being implemented, including enhanced oversight of recruitment and tighter controls on non-pay, consultancy, and professional-services expenditure.
It would be premature to speculate on the final year-end outturn. The final position will depend on the impact of the expenditure controls and savings measures currently being implemented across the health service.
The Government expects the HSE to take all possible action to manage expenditure within approved funding, while continuing to prioritise patient safety and essential services and maximising the benefit from the substantial public investment in healthcare.

question: Deputy Seán Crowe asked the Minister for Health to give an update on the working group established in 2024 to develop recommendations on a National Hearing Plan; if they have made a report and if the Minister intends it be made public; and the date by which a hearing care plan will be published and implemented.
reply:
The National Hearing Care Plan Working Group is jointly chaired by the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive (HSE). Membership of the Working Group is drawn from relevant stakeholders, including clinicians, representative bodies, and other agencies.
The Working Group has been tasked with developing recommendations for a holistic model of hearing care in Ireland. To support this, a structured workstream has been developed, focused on progressing priority issues. Significant progress has been made to date.
An important milestone in progressing the development of the Plan was a public consultation process. The views and opinions gathered through this process will directly inform the development and finalisation of the National Hearing Care Plan.
The draft Plan produced by the Group will be presented to the Minister by the end of the year for approval prior to publishing. Recommendations arising from the Plan will be implemented on a phased and priority basis.

reply:
Under the Health (Pricing and Supply of Medical Goods) Act 2013, the Health Service Executive (HSE) has statutory responsibility for decisions on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines.
To commence this process, a pharmaceutical company must submit an application for a new medicine or a new use of an existing medicine, which has been granted European Medicines Agency (EMA) or Health Products Regulatory Authority (HPRA) authorisation, to the HSE’s Corporate Pharmaceutical Unit.
Applicants must continue to engage throughout the process to ensure that the necessary evidence is available for the HSE to carry out its statutory role as a decision-maker with respect to the reimbursement of new medicines, in accordance with the Act. The Act specifies nine criteria which must be considered. These include the health needs of the public and the clinical need for the medicine. All these factors, taken together, allow the HSE to make an informed decision on new medicines.
The Drugs Group is the national committee which the HSE has in place to make recommendations on the pricing and reimbursement of medicines. The membership of the HSE Drugs Group includes public interest members. Pharmacoeconomic reports are reviewed by the HSE Drugs Group along with the outputs of commercial negotiations, and any patient group submission(s) received. The HSE Drugs Group considers all of the evidence and makes a recommendation to the HSE Senior Management Team.

question: Deputy William Aird asked the Minister for Health if she will introduce a publicly funded shingles vaccination programme, initially targeting adults aged 65 years and over and immunocompromised individuals, in line with the recommendations of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee; and if her Department has assessed the cost-effectiveness of a targeted programme for these groups, given the cost of private vaccination and the risk of serious complications, including long-term nerve pain.
reply:
The immunisation programme in Ireland is informed by the advice of the National Immunisation Advisory Committee (NIAC). NIAC considers the prevalence of the relevant disease in Ireland as well as international best practice in relation to immunisation when developing its advice
The current NIAC guidelines state that the shingles vaccine may be considered for those aged 65 years and older, due to the greater burden and severity of disease in this age group and in those aged 18 years and older at increased risk of shingles.
The Health Information and Quality Authority (HIQA) has carried out a Health Technology Assessment (HTA) on the herpes zoster vaccine which protects against shingles. A HTA is a multidisciplinary research process that collects and summarises information about a health technology. HIQA’s HTA examined the evidence on the clinical effectiveness and safety of shingles vaccines. The cost effectiveness and budget impact were also reviewed, along with the ethical, social and organisational implications of including the vaccine in the adult immunisation schedule.
HIQA published this HTA on 19 July 2024. The HTA found that adding the shingles vaccine to the routine immunisation schedule, at the vaccine price at the time, for all adults aged 65 years and over would not be cost effective and would be associated with a substantial budget impact.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Health if she is satisfied that sufficient data is being collected to assess any relationship between abortion and subsequent adverse mental health outcomes, including suicide; and whether consideration is being given to enhanced data collection in this area.
reply:
Under section 20 (1) of the Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018, a notification of each termination of pregnancy carried out under the legislation must be notified to the Minister for Health within 28 days of it being carried out.
Section 20, subsections (3) and (4), require the Minister to prepare a report on the notifications received in a given year not later than 30 June the following year and thereafter to lay it before the Houses of the Oireachtas and arrange for its publication.
The notifications are recorded on the form entitled “Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018 (Notifications) Regulations 2018” (Statutory Instrument No. 597 of 2018). The following information is included in the form:
• Medical Council registration number of the medical practitioner who carried out the termination of pregnancy.
• The section of the Act under which the termination was carried out, i.e., section 9, 10, 11 or 12.
• Medical Council registration number(s) of the medical practitioner(s) who made the certification concerned.
• The county of residence, or place of residence (where the woman resides outside of the State)
• The date on which the termination of pregnancy was carried out.
No further information is collected as part of this process.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality her views on whether existing legislation and regulations are sufficient to support workers that are seeking reasonable allowances for flexible working.
reply:
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 complements existing family leaves by providing additional flexibility to ensure that workers are supported in balancing their work and private lives.
The Act introduced important entitlements for workers, including five days leave for medical care purposes and an extension to the entitlement to breastfeeding breaks. It also introduced the right to request remote working for all employees and the right to request flexible working for parents and carers in line with Article 9 of the Directive EU 2019/1158.
Remote, hybrid and flexible working represent a significant opportunity for creating a more inclusive labour market and society, particularly for people with caring responsibilities, people returning to the workforce, older people, people with disabilities and people facing long commutes in the context of high fuel costs. This in turn provides employers with access to a larger talent pool, with remote and hybrid options representing powerful tools for staff recruitment and retention which improves economic performance and labour market access overall.
The Government is also prioritising further work-life balance measures through new National Strategy for Women and Girls 2025-2030, which was published on the 18th of November 2025, and includes a number of objectives to empower women in decision making and leadership roles, support women in and returning to the workforce and also to bring a much needed focus on sharin

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality whether she will review the 14-working-week statutory limit on the transfer of parental leave between qualifying parents employed by the same employer, having regard to the fact that the overall parental leave entitlement has increased to 26 working weeks; whether the retention of the 14-week limit following the increase in the overall entitlement was an intentional policy decision; and whether she intends to amend section 6(6A) of the Parental Leave Act 1998 to increase this limit.
reply:
There have been significant developments in entitlements for parents of working families in recent years.
Under the Parental Leave Acts, 26 weeks unpaid leave can be taken by an employee who is a relevant parent to take care of a child. It should be noted that the legislation only sets out the minimum entitlement to parental leave. Depending on an individual’s contract of employment, they may have more extensive rights to parental leave, as employers have the option to offer more than the entitlement set out in the legislation.
Both parents have an equal, separate entitlement to parental leave. Where both parents work for the same employer and the employer agrees, one parent can transfer 14 weeks of their parental leave entitlement to the other parent. This is to ensure that fathers as well as mothers are supported in their caring roles and to support women's equal labour market participation.
The Work Life Balance and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 2023 was enacted on 4 April 2023, and also introduces important entitlements for workers, including leave for medical care purposes for parents of children under 12, and the right to request flexible working for parents and carers. It transposes the Work-Life Balance Directive which specifically prevents the transfer of paid leave between parents in the interests of gender equality and of encouraging fathers as well as mothers to take such leave. question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality the communication that is taking place between her Department and the Health Service Executive regarding the regularisation of personalised budgets for persons with disabilities.
reply:
A personalised budget is a payment made in lieu of specialised disability support services that would otherwise be arranged or provided on the individual's behalf. Personalised budgets enable individuals to organise and manage their own support arrangements in a manner that best reflects their needs, preferences and goals.
Published in 2018, the report of the Taskforce on Personalised Budgets recommended that the Department of Health and the Health Service Executive should establish demonstration projects to test the delivery of personalised budgets in an Irish context with a view to identifying the best approach for the wider roll-out of the model following the initial demonstration phase.
The Personalised Budget Demonstrator Pilot was launched in August 2019 on a cost-neutral basis, with expressions of interest for participation sought from disabled adults in receipt of HSE funded specialist disability services.

The extension gives an opportunity for farmers to ensure they can comply with the closed period while also promoting responsible slurry application.

question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade her views that there are infringements on the right to protest in Germany in relation to the right of people to protest in solidarity with the Palestinian people.
reply:
The promotion and protection of human rights, including the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, are vital elements of Ireland’s foreign policy. Ireland consistently advocates for the protection of these rights internationally and encourages all States to uphold their obligations under international human rights law.
These principles guide all of our engagements with Germany.
Germany is a democratic constitutional state governed by the rule of law, where state authority is bound by the constitution, the law, and the justice system. Fundamental rights are protected through the German constitution as well as through Germany’s obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights, the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and other international instruments.

question: Deputy Alan Kelly asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration if he or his Department or any agencies, bodies or organisations under the aegis of his Department are aware of any instances where communications were intercepted in the State that were outside the legal provisions of the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) Act 1993; and, if so, the details of all instances.
reply:
As the Deputy is aware, in Ireland, lawful interception is governed by the Interception of Postal Packets and Telecommunications Messages (Regulation) 1993. The Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration may authorise bodies designated under the Act to lawfully intercept communications for the purposes of investigating serious crime or safeguarding the security of the State. Under section 6 of the Act, an application for authorisation of interception may be made by the Garda Commissioner, the Chief of Staff of the Defence Forces, or the Police Ombudsman.
Use of the 1993 Act is subject to a number of strict conditions including that investigations not involving interception have failed, or are likely to fail, to produce the necessary information or evidence; that the intelligence resulting from an interception would be of material assistance and that it is justified, notwithstanding the importance of preserving privacy.
Section 12 of the 1993 Act restricts disclosure in respect of lawful interception authorisations and it places a requirement on the Minister to ensure that such arrangements are in place to limit to the minimum necessary for the purpose of the prevention or detection of serious offences or in the interests of the security of the State, the disclosure of the fact that an authorisation has been given, and the contents of any communication which has been intercepted pursuant to an authorisation.

question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current status of the preparation of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship (Amendment) Bill 2026; the anticipated timeline for the publication of the Bill and its progression through the Houses of the Oireachtas; when pre-legislative scrutiny is expected to be undertaken; whether a public consultation will be conducted as part of the preparation of the legislation.
reply:
The 2025 Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer migration system that, amongst other things, protects the integrity of our immigration framework.
As Deputies may recall, last November, the Government approved a package of policy and legislative reforms to Ireland’s migration, citizenship, and naturalisation system, ensuring it is rules-based, efficient and more closely aligned with those of other EU Member States.
Government, at its meeting of 9 September, approved the priority drafting of legislation to amend aspects of the Irish Naturalisation and Citizenship Act 1956.
The General Scheme of the Bill has now been published and the General Scheme has been referred to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for pre-legislative scrutiny. The scheduling and management of pre-legislative scrutiny is a matter for the Oireachtas Committee.
Work is ongoing with the Office of Parliamentary Council to progress drafting and publication of the Bill as priority in this parliamentary session.

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration whether time spent residing in the State under temporary protection will be reckonable towards the proposed residency requirement for naturalisation under the Irish Nationality and Citizenship (Amendment) Bill 2026.
reply:
The Government recognises and values the significant contribution that migrants make to Irish society, communities and the economy.
The Programme for Government contains a commitment to continue to implement a firmer and more sustainable migration system which protects the integrity of the State's immigration framework. In that context, the General Scheme of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Bill 2026 proposes a number of reforms to the citizenship process.
Citizenship represents the fullest expression of membership of Irish society and it is important that the legislative framework governing access to citizenship is robust, fair and sustainable. The proposed changes do not seek to restrict integration or exclude migrants from Irish society. Rather, they are intended to ensure that citizenship reflects a genuine and lasting connection to Ireland, an understanding of the State and its institutions, and an ongoing commitment to Irish society.
The proposed amendments relate to the conditions for acquiring citizenship and do not affect a person's entitlement to reside, work, study, establish a business or build a life in Ireland in accordance with the terms of their immigration permission.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the actions he is taking to regulate the gambling sector in the context of reports indicating that Ireland has some of the highest rates of gambling in the world (details supplied); and the measures in place to prevent the targeting of vulnerable gambling addicts by betting companies.
reply:
The Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (the Act) establishes a comprehensive framework for the licensing and regulation of betting, gaming, and certain lotteries, including activities provided online to persons in the State. It also establishes a new, independent statutory body, the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). Last year, I signed orders to commence the first provisions of the Act and to establish the GRAI from 5 March 2025.
At its core, the Act is a public health measure aimed at protecting citizens from gambling harm, particularly children, young people, and those in our communities who are more vulnerable.
In February of this year, I signed a commencement order for key elements of the Act, including the enforcement and complaints functions that underpin the new licensing framework. The order confers robust investigative powers on the GRAI and allows for administrative sanctions in the form of fines of up to €20 million, or 10% of a licensee’s turnover, whichever is greater, to be imposed on licensees found to be in contravention of the Act. A number of criminal enforcement powers have also been commenced, as have provisions allowing the GRAI to apply to the High Court for an order directing illegal operators to cease operations.

• the continuation of prohibitions on allowing a child to gamble;

question: Deputy Sinéad Gibney asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade whether she has advocated for the use of the EU blocking mechanism to protect US citizens in Europe facing sanctions from the Trump administration.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 38 and 51 together.
Ireland is a strong supporter of the International Criminal Court (ICC), which we view as the cornerstone of the international system of criminal justice. I deeply regret the imposition of US sanctions against thirteen officials of the ICC. Such measures threaten to corrode the international legal order on which all states – but particularly small states like Ireland – depend.
I am aware of ongoing reports that the United States is considering sanctioning the ICC as an institution, which would very significantly impede the operational capacity of the Court. The ICC must be allowed to continue its important work, independently and impartially.
Ireland has been consistent in calling for all measures against the ICC to be withdrawn. The Taoiseach reiterated this principled position during his address to the UN General Assembly during UN High Level Week on 24 September.
The Government believes that a coordinated EU response is the most effective way to protect the ICC and its officials. In our role as President of the EU Council, Ireland is committed to playing its part in maintaining full solidarity with the Court at this crucial moment.

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the reason he was not among the 22 of home affairs ministers who co-signed a letter calling for a special meeting of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council on 4 August 2026 to discuss the influx of illegal immigration into the Spanish territory of Cueta.
reply:
The letter referred to by the Deputy, sent on Saturday 1 August, was addressed to Ireland in our capacity as Presidency of the Council of the European Union, as well as to António Costa, President of the European Council and Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission.
Ireland, as Presidency of the Council of the European Union, responded by convening an extraordinary meeting of Ministers of the Interior on 4 August, which I chaired.
I can assure the Deputy that Ireland, as Presidency, has acted decisively and quickly in response to the situation in Ceuta, and we continue to do so.
In addition to responding to the request to convene an extraordinary meeting of Interior Ministers to discuss the situation, we have hosted a number of senior official, and ambassador level meetings. We continue to engage with Spain and the European Commission to ensure that Spain is supported as it manages this challenging situation.
Alongside this, we are working to advance a number of pieces of work identified by Ministers on 4 August as priority actions which will better equip the Union to prevent and manage any similar future incidents.
At the Justice and Home Affairs Council today (01 October) I brought forward proposals to advance two of these priority actions, both of which were welcomed by Ministers. question: Deputy Rose Conway-Walsh asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has begun any internal planning concerning future constitutional change.
reply:
The Programme for Government states clearly that this Government is committed to the unity of the Irish people. This can only be achieved through a sustained focus on and investment in reconciliation. We remain steadfast in implementing the Good Friday Agreement in full and supporting the function of all of its institutions.
Our commitment is backed by our Shared Island Initiative, to which we have allocated €2 billion through to 2035.
The Initiative is enabling the largest-ever programme of all-island investment across all sectors, to build a more connected island, in terms of infrastructure, services, our economy and, crucially, between people.
The Shared Island Initiative is just one part of our work to promote peace and reconciliation on this island, work that also includes my Department's Reconciliation Fund, which awards grants to organisations working to build better relations within and between traditions in Northern Ireland, between North and South, and between Ireland and Britain. My Department also supports and provides the Dublin Secretariat for the International Fund for Ireland which continues to do important work in Northern Ireland and the border counties.
The Government is working to build a more prosperous and reconciled island for people North and South, and in the event of a future referendum, we will make all necessary preparations, in accordance with the terms of the Constitution and the principles and procedures of the Agreement.

question: Deputy Ryan O'Meara asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department has plans to review or amend the 18.5 hour limitation for carer's allowance.
reply:
The main income supports for family carers provided by my Department are Carer’s Allowance, Carer’s Benefit, Domiciliary Care Allowance and the Carer’s Support Grant. Spending on these payments is expected to amount to over €2.2 billion in 2026.
Carer’s Allowance is an income support payment for people who are providing full-time care and attention to someone who needs significant support due to age, disability or illness. The purpose of the scheme is to support people whose capacity to earn an income is reduced because of their caring responsibilities.
To qualify for Carer's Allowance, Carer's Benefit or the Carer's Support Grant, the carer must provide full-time care and attention.
A carer is considered to be providing full-time care and attention to a relevant person, where the number of hours providing such care is not less than 35 hours in a period of seven consecutive days, and care is provided on any five days, whether consecutive or not, within a period of seven consecutive days.
While these payments are based on the provision of full-time care and attention by the carer, the statutory qualifying conditions allow carers to engage in work, training or education up to 18.5 hours per week. This threshold was increased from 15 hours as part of Budget 2020 following feedback from carers and carers' organisations who found the 15 hour limit too restrictive. During this time, adequate provision must be made for the care of the relevant person.

question: Deputy Seán Ó Fearghaíl asked the Minister for Social Protection If he will address the concerns raised in correspondence (details supplied) regarding the financial pressures facing carers and low-income households experiencing energy arrears; if he will outline the supports currently available in such circumstances; and to indicate whether any additional measures are under consideration.
reply:

According to the latest CSO data, there are just over 1.8 million households in Ireland. Of these, 463,910 households are eligible for the Fuel Allowance scheme, representing approximately 26% of all households nationwide.

This added an additional €152 to households in most need of support and increased the fuel season amount to €1,216 in 2026. The estimated expenditure on the scheme in 2026 is €557.4 million.

question: Deputy Ken O'Flynn asked the Minister for Social Protection if his Department will review the income thresholds for the working family payment as they apply to lone parent households, including whether childcare costs could be taken into account in the means assessment; the estimated cost of increasing the thresholds by 5% and 10% respectively.
reply:
The Working Family Payment is a tax-free income support designed to prevent in-work poverty for low paid employees with child dependents, and to offer a financial incentive to take-up employment.
As of August 2026, there were 56,777 families in receipt of Working Family Payment. Lone parents in receipt of Working Family Payment are assessed against the same income thresholds as two-parent families.
It is difficult to provide a costing for a 5% and 10% increase to each Working Family Payment threshold, as this would require costing a different threshold increase for each household size. A 5% increase to the €765 threshold would equate to a €38.25 increase in the threshold while a 10% increase would equate to €76.50 increase to the threshold. If these increases were applied across the thresholds for all family sizes, the estimated cost of the €38.25 increase would be €61 million per year, while an increase of €76.50 would cost approximately €122 million per year.
There are no current plans to take childcare costs into consideration into the income assessment for Working Family Payment. All other matters in relation to childcare are under the responsibility of the Minister for Children, Disability and Equality.
Decisions regarding social welfare rates and thresholds are considered as part of the annual Budget process, having regard to the overall budgetary package, available resources and Government priorities.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will increase the savings threshold in respect of disregard for non contributory pension applicants.
reply:
Social welfare legislation provides that means tests take account of the income and assets of the person (and their spouse or partner) applying for the relevant scheme. The means assessment includes income from sources such as employment, self-employment, and occupational pensions. It also includes property owned, other than the family home, and capital such as savings, shares, and other investments.
The means assessment for a personal rate of the State Pension (Non-contributory) is as follows: the first €20,000 (or €40,000 for a couple) of capital an applicant holds is fully disregarded; the next €10,000 is assessed at €1 per thousand, the next €10,000 is assessed at €2 per thousand, with the remainder assessed at €4 per thousand. Under this system people with capital assets of up to €111,000 - excluding the value of their family home - can still receive a partial pension payment.
The assessment of capital reflects an expectation that people with reasonable amounts of capital and property are in a position to use that capital, to support themselves without having to rely solely on a means-tested welfare payment.
The use of means tests, including the assessment of capital assets, is important in targeting State funded supports to people who have greatest need and avoiding the provision of such supports to people who with significant assets or income.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Social Protection the action he will take to engage with a school meals provider in relation to their concerns on the viability of the current payment model (detail supplied); and if he will meet with them to work through these concerns.
reply:
All 3,200 primary schools and 550,000 children are eligible for hot school meals. Across all meal types there some 3,700 schools and 682,000 children are eligible for support. This equates to the distribution of up to 3.4 million school meals per week. The budget for 2026 is €286 million.
The dinner option available under the School Meals Programme for DEIS Secondary schools was developed and tendered on the basis that meals would be prepared on-site utilising the canteen/kitchen facilities available in those schools. In contrast, the Hot School Meals Scheme introduced in 2019 was specifically developed for Primary Schools. Recognising that the vast majority of primary schools do not have catering facilities the funding model is calibrated to allow for off-site preparation and delivery to the schools.
Secondary schools issued requests for tenders based on the payment rates available, rates that were well known among interested suppliers within the food services industry. If a company is using the ‘pre-prepared’ Hot School Meal delivery model in the secondary schools concerned this was a business decision made by them when tendering for the contract.
The rate for the dinner model was increased in 2023 when there was an increase for all options under the School Meals Programme. There are no plans for a further increase at this time.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

question: Deputy Brendan Smith asked the Minister for Social Protection if he will give detailed and favourable consideration in respect of a sizeable increase in the living alone allowance payment.
reply:
The Living Alone Increase is an additional weekly payment made to people who live alone and are in receipt of a qualifying social welfare payment. It is available to people aged 66 and over receiving a State Pension, Bereaved Partner’s Pension, Deserted Wife’s Benefit, Incapacity Supplement or certain Occupational Injuries benefits. It is also available to people aged under 66 in receipt of Disability Allowance, Invalidity Pension, Blind Pension or Incapacity Supplement. The current rate is €22 per week.
The Living Alone Increase is not a stand-alone payment and is therefore payable only to people receiving a qualifying social welfare payment. Approximately 260,000 people currently receive the increase.
The purpose of the payment is to recognise that people living alone must meet the cost of running and maintaining a household from a single income. It therefore provides additional support to pensioners and people with disabilities or long-term illness who may be particularly vulnerable to financial pressures.
The Living Alone Increase has risen from €9 per week in 2019 to €22 today, an increase of 144%. Core social welfare rates have increased by €51 per week over the same period. Budget 2026 provided for a €10 increase in most weekly social welfare payments, together with other targeted measures to assist households.

question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Social Protection the steps he will take to address the situation whereby a carer receiving State pension is only eligible for half rate carers payment.
reply:

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether it is the intention of the Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026 that a social housing application may be refused where the lead applicant satisfies the legal and habitual residency requirements set out in section 20A(1), but a dependent child, dependent adult or connected person included in the application does not; and whether guidance has issued or will issue to housing authorities on this matter.
reply:
The Housing and Residential Tenancies (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2026, provides for lawful residency and habitual residency as an eligibility criteria for social housing.
Preparations are underway for the commencement of the new statutory arrangements, including detailed guidance on how housing authorities should assess lawful and habitual residency requirements.
Under the Act, a household shall not be eligible for social housing support unless at the time of carrying out the social housing assessment, each member of the household is lawfully resident in the State and each member of the household is habitually resident in the State in accordance with Section 20A.
The lawful residency requirement does not apply to a member of the household who is a child within the meaning of the Children Act 2001. However, a child who forms part of the applicant household must be habitually resident in the State.
Households deemed ineligible for social housing may reapply and be reassessed for support at any stage, subject to meeting the eligibility and need criteria at the point at which they apply. Decisions on the qualification of households for social housing support, the most appropriate form of such support, and the allocation of that support are a matter solely for the local authority concerned.

question: Deputy Conor Sheehan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage his view on the recent analysis published by the Before We Die campaign, which indicates that local authorities held a combined total of €1.53 billion in unspent development contributions in 2024; and the steps he is taking to ensure these capital funds are urgently activated to deliver critical housing infrastructure.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 352 to 354, inclusive, together.
Firstly, I must outline that the questions misunderstand the position regarding both the allowable uses of development contributions and the figures quoted in respect of same.
Development contributions allow local authorities to recoup some of the public costs of servicing land for private development. They provide a mechanism for contributions to the cost of providing public infrastructure and facilities that benefit development in the area and may be spent on public infrastructure defined under the Planning Acts. These include the provision of open spaces, recreational and community facilities, roads, surface water sewers, public transport, school sites, broadband and flood relief works. There is currently no provision in the Planning Acts allowing the use of development contributions in respect of the direct construction of housing. However, development contributions may be used for the provision of public infrastructure that supports housing development (for example road infrastructure, open space provision, etc).
The collection and expenditure of development contributions is governed by planning legislation in the first instance and locally devised development contribution schemes in the second instance.

question: Deputy Donna McGettigan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to confirm that foundations will be included in the current review under section 51 of the DCB Act 2022; when the review is due to be completed; and when he will report the findings to the house.
reply:
The Remediation of Dwellings Damaged by the use of Defective Concrete Blocks Act 2022 as amended by the Act of 2025 sets out the framework under which the Grant Scheme which provides grant funding to people whose homes have been affected by Defective Concrete Blocks operates.
A number of amendments contained in the 2025 Act came into operation on 25 February 2026 and more recently further provisions commenced on 27 May 2026.
On 2 June 2026, the National Standards Authority Ireland published a revised standard - I.S. 465:2026. As per Section 51 of the 2022 Act, a review of the operation of the Act has now been commenced and is being carried out by my Department with the assistance of external expertise.
The review will make recommendations regarding several aspects of the Act and their interaction with the Defective Concrete Blocks Grant Scheme. While foundations are not currently provided for under the Grant Scheme, they will be considered as part of the review.
The review is progressing. Following its completion, I will report to each House of the Oireachtas, setting out the findings and conclusions arising from the review, in accordance with the requirements of the Act.
It is not possible to provide a timeframe for its completion at this point in time. However, the work will continue to be progressed as quickly as possible.

question: Deputy Peter Roche asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the engagement his Department has had with stakeholders regarding the availability of long-term rental accommodation and the impact of short-term lets on supply.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 349 and 350 together.
The Department of Enterprise, Tourism and Employment (DETE) has drafted the Short Term Letting and Tourism (STLT) Bill General Scheme in full alignment with the EU Short Term Rental Regulation. The introduction of the STLT Bill will provide a more effective legal and administrative basis to regulate short term lettings. This Bill when enacted will provide the statutory basis for the introduction of a register for all Short Term Lettings in Ireland, which will be implemented and managed by Fáilte Ireland.
I am advised by DETE that Fáilte Ireland estimates that approximately 32,060 STL properties were advertised online in the State in August 2026. Up to 57% were listed as entire houses or apartments.
In line with the proposed introduction of DETE’s STLT Bill, all short-term letting accommodation providers will be required to register with Fáilte Ireland. As part of the registration process, accommodation providers will need to confirm that they are planning compliant.
The Planning Acts provide that the short-term letting of a residential property is a material change of use of the property concerned, thereby requiring planning permission, unless otherwise specifically exempted. question: Deputy Gillian Toole asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage if the housing assistance payment scheme will be extended to include the housing-asset owning parents of persons with additional needs or disabilities.
reply:
The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) Scheme is deemed to be a social housing support under the Housing (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 2014 and an assessment of housing need must be completed in order for a household to qualify for HAP. Any household with an identified housing need is eligible for HAP.
In order for housing assistance to be provided under the Act the housing authority must be satisfied that the tenancy concerned is or would be a tenancy in good faith. Where there is a family relationship between the tenant and the landlord, the housing authority may seek evidence of a previous landlord and tenant relationship in respect of the property. This evidence may include:
• Proof of rent payments;
• A lease or tenancy agreement for the property; and
• Registration of the tenancy with the Residential Tenancies Board.
In order for a housing authority to be satisfied that a tenancy is or would be in good faith; the onus is on the applicant and landlord to prove that what is being proposed is a bona fide tenancy. Ultimately, it is the responsibility of the housing authority to make a decision in each individual case.
HAP support is available to tenants in rent a room scheme arrangements; however, the rental of a room to a civil partner, son or daughter are excluded from this scheme. HAP cannot be paid where the tenant is seeking to rent within the family home, including the curtilage of the family home. HAP payments cannot be paid on homes that are acquired by family member

question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the funding schemes that may be available to support restoration works at the historic boundary wall at Seir Kieran Cemetery, Clareen, Birr, County Offaly; and whether projects of this nature would be eligible for consideration under the built heritage investment scheme, and the historic structures fund or any other relevant heritage conservation programmes.
reply:
The Community Monuments Fund (CMF) is administered by my Department through the Local Authorities and the call for applications for the 2027 scheme will be announced in the coming weeks.
The Community Monuments Fund provides funding for projects in relation to:
(i) Archaeological Monuments that are included in the Record of Monuments and Places (RMP) under the National Monuments Act 1930 (as amended);
(ii) Archaeological Monuments that are identified in the Sites and Monuments Record compiled by the National Monuments Service.
The Built Heritage Investment Scheme (BHIS) and the Historic Structures Fund (HSF) are administered by my Department through the Local Authorities and both schemes are currently open. For BHIS, applications must be submitted to the Local Authority no later than 30 October 2026. For HSF, applications must be submitted to the Local Authority no later than 27 November 2026.
Full details about eligibility for both schemes may be found on gov.ie at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/services/built-heritage-investment-scheme-bhis/ and www.gov.ie/en/department-of-housing-local-government-and-heritage/services/historic-structures-fund/.
For applications to all of these schemes it is highly advisable to make contact with The Heritage Officer in the relevant Local Authority.

question: Deputy Pa Daly asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage to provide an update on the commitment to introduce solar planning guidelines in the Programme for Government; the timeline for delivery; if guidelines will be delivered by the end of 2026.
reply:
In line with commitments in the Programme for Government 2025, my Department is working with the Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment (DCEE), which holds policy responsibility for renewable energy matters, in respect of the introduction of a number of National Planning Statements related to Ireland's Climate Action Plan target to increase the share of electricity generated from renewable sources up to 80% in 2030. This includes the preparation of a National Planning Statement for solar energy development.
Further to the commencement of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of the Planning and Development Act 2024 on 2 October 2025, provisions for National Planning Statements have been introduced to replace the provisions for Ministerial guidelines issued under section 28 of the Planning and Development Act 2000. All existing Section 28 guidelines will, over time, be revoked and replaced with new National Planning Statements. Any current section 28 guidelines will however remain in force until revoked or replaced by a corresponding National Planning Statement. The timing of the issuing of National Planning Statements will be based on Government priorities.
In respect of sectoral national planning statements in particular there is also an important role for the relevant policy Department in collaborating with my Department on the development of these National Planning Statements. question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of social homes retrofitted to date and the number he expects to be retrofitted by 2030.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 178 and 344 together.
Since 2013, my Department’s Energy Efficiency Retrofit Programme (EERP) has supported the retrofit of 85,292 local authority owned social homes requiring insulation and energy efficiency upgrades, with more than €0.5 billion provided to local authorities to support these works in the period to end-2025.
A revised EERP, introduced in 2021, is targeting the retrofit 36,500 local authority homes by 2030 to a post works BER equivalent of the previous B2 standard (125 kWh/m²/year). Eligible works include insulation upgrades, replacement of windows and doors, heat pump installation and associated works. Since 2021, over 11,000 social homes have been upgraded, supported by more than €342 million provided by my Department in the period.
Some €140 million has been allocated to local authorities under the EERP this year. This represents an increase of more than 50% on the previous year's allocation and is expected to facilitate the retrofit of approximately 3,500 social homes.
A year-by-year breakdown of funding and completed retrofits for 2013-2025 is available on my Department’s website at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/668c1-energy-efficiency-retrofitting-programme-expenditure-output/
Details of the Midlands Energy Retrofit Pilot Programme are available at: www.gov.ie/en/publication/b86b3-midlands-energy-retrofit-programme-expenditure-and-units/#

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage whether he has engaged with local authorities on rates schemes for vacant buildings to encourage new enterprise.
reply:
Local authorities have been levying and collecting rates under the Local Government Rates and Other Matters Act 2019 since 1 January 2024. The Act expanded the range of measures available to local authorities to support local businesses and address specific local economic challenges.
Section 9 of the Act provides for the introduction of rates vacancy abatement schemes. These schemes afford local authorities considerable flexibility in developing targeted interventions for vacant commercial properties. In determining the design of such schemes, local authorities may take account of local economic conditions, the extent and nature of commercial vacancy, and wider regeneration objectives. Vacancy abatement schemes may be tailored to particular towns, geographic areas, classes of property or categories of ratepayer. The introduction and operation of any such scheme is a matter for the elected members of the local authority.
Section 15 of the Act enables local authorities to make rates waiver schemes in support of local and national policy objectives. This provision further enhances the capacity of local authorities and elected members to respond to the particular needs and challenges of their areas.
A waiver scheme may be introduced where it supports the implementation of:
• the National Planning Framework;
• a local area plan;
• a local economic and community plan; or
• an urban area plan, priority area plan or coordinated area plan.

question: Deputy Thomas Gould asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the role his Department is taking in the Butter Exchange Project in Cork city.
reply:
THRIVE (Town Centre First Heritage Revival) Scheme is a grant scheme of c. €120million for local authorities which is co-funded by the Government and the European Union and delivered under Ireland’s two ERDF (European Regional Development Fund) Regional Programmes. The THRIVE Scheme provides funding for the preparation of Town Centre First Plans, strategies and project development work in towns to enable future capital funding applications to be made to Government for the identified projects in these plans. THRIVE also supports town regeneration through direct capital funding of €115 million in total for the implementation of identified heritage-related projects in town centres – with 19 projects currently being funded across the country.
The Shandon Exchange, located in Shandon, Cork City, comprises of the Butter Exchange Building and the adjacent Weighmaster’s House which have been derelict for a number of years. Both properties will be regenerated to ensure the conservation and future safeguarding of the building complex. Cork City Council forecast a total project cost of €11.5 million. €7m of this will be funded by the THRIVE award and €4.5 million will be funded by Cork City Council.
Further Details are available here: www.corkcity.ie/en/council-services/services/planning/thrive/.

question: Deputy Micheál Carrigy asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport the specific timeline for the notification of successful applicants under the basic income for the arts (2026–2029) scheme, which closed for applications on 12 May 2026; the exact date when applicants will be informed of the selection outcome; the precise date when the first backdated weekly payments of €325 will reach the accounts of successful recipients.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 300, 301, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315, 316, 319, 321, 322, 323, 324, 326, 327, 328, 329, 331, 332, 333, 334, 335, 336, 337, 338, 339, 340 and 341 together.
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The selection process took place in May with independent oversight by EY. The selection ranked all applications from 1 - 10,000 and eligibility checks then started from the first selected applicant to determine if those selected were eligible. That assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive

question: Deputy Duncan Smith asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade if her Department has engaged with the German Government in regard to persons (details supplied).
reply:

I am following developments in this consular case very closely and will continue to do so. I would like to acknowledge that this is a difficult time for the citizen and the family.

My Department, in particular our Consulate General in Munich, supported by our Embassy in Berlin and the Consular Directorate here in Dublin, has been providing consular assistance to the citizen since September 2025, when we were first notified of the case. question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on Ireland's EU Presidency; and the way in which Irish priorities are being advanced.
reply:
Ireland assumed the Presidency of the Council of the European Union on 1 July and will hold this role until 31 December 2026. Since the start of our term, we have made substantial progress in advancing policy objectives across our three core priorities of competitiveness, values and security.
Early achievements include renewed momentum on EU enlargement, including chairing the largest number of accession conferences held in a single day in over twenty years. We secured agreement on further packages of sanctions against Russia, and the extension of temporary protection for those fleeing Ukraine. We have made important progress on measures to better protect children from sexual abuse online. We are advancing significant measures aimed at strengthening Europe’s competitiveness.
That means making it easier for Irish and European businesses to grow, invest and create jobs. We are committed to protecting children online, supporting our farmers and rural communities, strengthening Europe’s security and standing firmly with Ukraine. And we are making every effort to ensure that the European Union remains competitive in a rapidly changing global economy.
We are delivering a successful programme of Presidency meetings, both in Brussels and here in Ireland, which has helped to strengthen relationships and to move our agenda forward.
Communities across Ireland are hosting large numbers of European visitors and are showcasing all that Ireland has to offer to our European partners. Through

I propose to take Questions Nos. 300, 301, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315, 316, 319, 321, 322, 323, 324, 326, 327, 328, 329, 331, 332, 333, 334, 335, 336, 337, 338, 339, 340 and 341 together.
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The selection process took place in May with independent oversight by EY. The selection ranked all applications from 1 - 10,000 and eligibility checks then started from the first selected applicant to determine if those selected were eligible. That assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive

question: Deputy Albert Dolan asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to provide a breakdown of successful school-related applications under the three most recent completed rounds of the CSFF and its predecessor, the Sports Capital & Equipment Programme, specifying the school, county, partner sports club or organisation, project description, amount allocated and amount drawn down; the requirements for schools applying under the forthcoming round, including joint applications, facility-sharing agreements and community access; and whether his Department provides school-specific guidance or case studies of successful applications, in tabular form.
reply:
The provision of sports facilities in school settings is primarily the responsibility of the Minister for Education and Youth and the school governing authorities.
The information requested encompasses multiple rounds of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF) and is presently being collated by my Department. A report will be forwarded directly to the Deputy as soon as it is finalised. Details of all CSFF allocations are available on the Department's website at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-culture-communications-and-sport/collections/sports-capital-programme-allocations/.
I have also recently met with officials from the Department of Education and Youth to discuss how the benefits for sporting organisations and schools from working together on CSFF applications can be optimised and there has been subsequent further engagement between officials from both Departments.
A new online grant management system for CSFF, SPRAOI, went live on Monday 28 September for registrations; any clubs or organisations that are not already registered with the Department may do so now.
The window for funding applications will run from Monday 19 October 2026 to Friday 26 February 2027.

question: Deputy Donnchadh Ó Laoghaire asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update on her Department's recent engagements with the Government of Ukraine in relation to the ongoing conflict.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 30 and 32 together.
Ireland’s support to Ukraine is unwavering and remains a key focus of my engagements with my EU counterparts, both bilaterally and in Brussels. This war and the threat posed by Russia is not only an existential issue for Ukraine but is a major challenge to the security of Europe.
During our EU Presidency, Ireland is working with our EU and international partners in support of Ukraine and efforts to secure a just, comprehensive and lasting peace.
We were honoured to host President Zelenskyy in Ireland on the first day of our Presidency. The Taoiseach visited Kyiv on 23 July to express Ireland’s continued support for Ukraine.
Russia’s aggression features prominently at each meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council. Ukraine was a key focus of the first meeting of our Presidency on 13 July, including an event I co-hosted with the High Representative to focus on civilian detainees in Ukraine’s occupied territories.
During this event, EU foreign ministers held an informal exchange over breakfast with Ukraine’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, as well as representatives of two Ukrainian human rights organisations that focus on the issue.
The Council then discussed Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, following an initial address by Minister Sybiha, who gave an overview of the situation on the ground and Ukraine’s most urgent needs.
The ensuing ministerial discussions focused on Ukraine's energy preparedness ahead

question: Deputy Michael Cahill asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade given that Ireland has presidency of the EU, if she will do everything possible to end the conflict and genocide in Gaza.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 14, 31 and 44 together.
Ireland continues to use every opportunity at the EU level and internationally to stress our grave concerns about the catastrophic humanitarian situation in Gaza, and ongoing Israeli operations in both Gaza and the West Bank. During Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU, we are working to maintain this focus at EU level. The situation in Gaza and the West Bank was discussed at the Informal Meeting of EU Foreign Ministers that I hosted in Wicklow last month. Ireland continues to press for appropriate EU action in response to egregious Israeli breaches of international law, human rights and democratic principles.
The situation in Palestine was a central focus of my engagement with EU and other international partners during High Level Week at the UN last week. Ireland participated in a number of events focused on Israel and Palestine, including the meeting jointly organised by France, the UK and Canada one year on from the New York Declaration. I attended the High-Level meeting of the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two State Solution, as well as a High Level event on International Humanitarian Law.

I propose to take Questions Nos. 300, 301, 303, 304, 305, 306, 307, 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315, 316, 319, 321, 322, 323, 324, 326, 327, 328, 329, 331, 332, 333, 334, 335, 336, 337, 338, 339, 340 and 341 together.
In February this year I announced that the Government had approved a permanent successor to the Basic Income for the Arts pilot scheme and that 2,000 artists would be provided with funding of €325 per week for three years. This is a major milestone for the arts in Ireland and I am particularly pleased that the research my Department conducted provided Government with a clear evidence base upon which to make that decision.
The deadline for application to the Basic Income for the Arts 2026 - 2029 was 5pm on Tuesday 12th May, with over 10,000 applications received by the deadline.
Like the pilot scheme selection is via an anonymous random selection process, this is considered the fairest method where there is not enough funding for all eligible applicants. The selection process took place in May with independent oversight by EY. The selection ranked all applications from 1 - 10,000 and eligibility checks then started from the first selected applicant to determine if those selected were eligible. That assessment process is ongoing to determine the final 2,000 applicants who will receive the BIA.
I appreciate that applicants are eager to know the outcome, however, in order to protect the integrity of the scheme the assessment process is by necessity very intensive

question: Deputy Seán Kyne asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport to confirm specifically that the Kingston Park and Millers Lane application remains eligible for consideration from additional funding under the 2024 LSSIF round; to confirm its status on his Department's reserve list; and whether the granting of full planning approval by An Coimisiún Pleanála will now be reflected in his Department's assessment of the project's readiness and deliverability.
reply:
The Large-Scale Sports Infrastructure Fund (LSSIF) was established under the National Sports Policy to provide Exchequer support for larger sports facility projects, typically those requiring investments greater than the maximum available under the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF).
The 2024 round of LSSIF received an unprecedented demand for funding, amounting to €665 million from 96 applicants. As a result of this significant demand, a range of valid applications, including the application referred to by the Deputy, did not receive an LSSIF allocation at the allocation stage.
It should be noted that, should additional funding become available, eligible applications that did not receive funding under the 2024 round and whose proposed projects align with key strategic national priorities and strategies such as the National Swimming Strategy could be considered for funding support in advance of a future round of the LSSIF.
With regard to a future round of the LSSIF, my current focus is on ensuring project delivery under the first two rounds of the LSSIF, 2018 and 2024, and this process will inform any decisions regarding the timing of the next round of LSSIF funding.

question: Deputy Shay Brennan asked the Minister for Foreign Affairs and Trade for a report on the discussions on Ukraine at the most recent EU Foreign Affairs council.
reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 30 and 32 together.
Ireland’s support to Ukraine is unwavering and remains a key focus of my engagements with my EU counterparts, both bilaterally and in Brussels. This war and the threat posed by Russia is not only an existential issue for Ukraine but is a major challenge to the security of Europe.
During our EU Presidency, Ireland is working with our EU and international partners in support of Ukraine and efforts to secure a just, comprehensive and lasting peace.
We were honoured to host President Zelenskyy in Ireland on the first day of our Presidency. The Taoiseach visited Kyiv on 23 July to express Ireland’s continued support for Ukraine.
Russia’s aggression features prominently at each meeting of the Foreign Affairs Council. Ukraine was a key focus of the first meeting of our Presidency on 13 July, including an event I co-hosted with the High Representative to focus on civilian detainees in Ukraine’s occupied territories.
During this event, EU foreign ministers held an informal exchange over breakfast with Ukraine’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, as well as representatives of two Ukrainian human rights organisations that focus on the issue.
The Council then discussed Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, following an initial address by Minister Sybiha, who gave an overview of the situation on the ground and Ukraine’s most urgent needs.
The ensuing ministerial discussions focused on Ukraine's energy preparedness ahead

question: Deputy Robert Troy asked the Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport if there are circumstances when a club (details supplied) can qualify for tier 2 CCSF funding; and if this element is reserved for regional applications.
reply:
My Department is currently preparing for the next round of the Community Sport Facilities Fund (CSFF), which I expect to open soon. A new online grant management system for CSFF, SPRAOI, went live on Monday 28 September for registrations. Any clubs or organisations that are not already registered with the Department may do so from that date.
The Department has collated extensive feedback from sporting clubs and organisations as an input to the key changes in the new 2026 round. The terms and conditions for the next CSFF round, and the timing of the application window, can be found on the Department's website. Regional Tier 2 Grant funding is only available to Local authorities and NGBs.
A wide reaching information campaign will be undertaken to assist clubs in any queries that have in relation to the application. The 2026 round will prioritise areas and sports that have been under-invested in over the years.

question: Deputy Barry Ward asked the Minister for Education and Youth if her attention has been drawn to concerns raised by PME students in relation to the structuring of their course and confusion related to qualifying modules (details supplied).
reply:
The Teaching Council is the body with the statutory authority and responsibility for the regulation of the teaching profession in Ireland including the registration of teachers in the State.
The Teaching Council registers teachers under the Teaching Council Act 2001-2015 (www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2001/act/8/enacted/en/htm) and in line with the Teaching Council Registration Regulations, 2025 (www.teachingcouncil.ie/assets/uploads/2025/10/SI.2025.0482_TC_Registration_Regulations.pdf). As set out in the Schedule of the Regulations, the Council registers teachers under five routes of registration: Route 1 - Primary, Route 2 - Post-primary, Route 3 - Further Education, Route 4 - Other and Route 5 - Student Teacher. question: Deputy Malcolm Byrne asked the Minister for Education and Youth the supports available for the installation of electric vehicle charging points at schools.
reply:
My Departments Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS) provides funding to schools for the provision of Electric Vehicle Chargers.
In March 2025, my Department announced the roll out of a new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme (CASWS). The CASWS (which was previously named the Summer Works Scheme) placed a strong emphasis on sustainability. Schools can now undertake additional measures such as insulation upgrades, LED lighting installation, EV charger provision, bike rack facilities to support active travel and other climate-focused works alongside traditional maintenance.
The CASWS enables individual school authorities to undertake small-scale building works on a devolved basis that, ideally, can be carried out during the summer months or at other times that avoid disrupting the operation of the school. The CASWS operates on a multi-annual basis across a number of categories of works.
The scheme opened for applications on the 1st May and the application window closed on the 30th of June 2025, with over 1400 applications being received. In November 2025, my Department announced the first tranche of approvals under the new Climate Action Summer Works Scheme. 297 projects were approved to proceed and involve primary, post primary and special schools, along with projects in all counties and across all categories of works.
It is anticipated that the next tranche of approvals will be announced in October 2026.

reply:
The project referred to by the Deputy is a campus project and is devolved for delivery to Galway and Roscommon Education and Training Board (GRETB).

The current status of all projects continues to be set out under item number ten at the following link: www.gov.ie. This is updated on a regular basis to reflect project progress through the various stages of capital appraisal, site acquisition, design, tender and construction.
